title: In Praise of Improvisation
Democratizing Wealth, Democratizing Power
abstract: Popular accounts of American historical development suggest that American politics are fundamentally cyclical, swinging back and forth between periods of reform and retrenchment.Following this theory — an idea espoused by prominent liberals such as Arthur Schlesinger Jr. — the re election of Barack Obama should have been cause not just for short-term exultation at the defeat of Mitt Romney and the far Right, but also sustained excitement that a reform agenda has been given four more years.In reality, few progressives feel this way. The net result of Obama’s re election is a perpetuation of the status quo in Washington — a grid-locked Congress that has bought hook, line, and sinker into deficit hysteria, thereby all but guaranteeing that the next several years will continue to be marked by high unemployment, austerity, and painful cuts at the local, state, and federal levels. Disturbingly, this climate is likely to foster widespread disillusionment with the capacity of progressive political leadership to produce meaningful change.Could Obama have done better with the hand he was dealt, going back to 2009? Some observers argue that he could have gone for a bigger, better-crafted stimulus clearly tied to concrete, visible infrastructure projects on a large enough scale to bring down unemployment more rapidly and, in doing so, averted the loss of Democratic control in Congress in 2010. Perhaps by prioritizing economic recovery over health care, he could have short-circuited the Tea Party and maintained control over the political agenda. Others say Obama should get more credit for helping to avert a depression and for passing a health care bill that, while flawed, at least goes a long way toward establishing the principle of universal health care as a right.But what if this debate about Obama is largely beside the point? The correct question to ask is not whether Obama could have done better (he could have), but what the frustrations of the Obama era teach us about the capacity of liberal politics to deliver meaningful change — even with a charismatic, intelligent president at the helm.Poverty has gone up, not down, over the past five years. The nation still has no meaningful policy, let alone a comprehensive strategy, for addressing climate change. Labor is still flat on its back as a force in the nation’s economic life. The defense and security budgets still command an exorbitant share of resources. Obama’s health care bill, though it has important progressive elements, does too little to tackle the cost inefficiencies associated with a private insurance–based system. The nation’s politics are as dominated by money as ever, and the Right has become even more extreme on many issues. Central cities remain largely neglected, investments in public transit and green technology have been minuscule relative to need, and pressing needs for affordable housing are going unmet on a mass scale. The picture is even grimmer for states and localities grappling with impossible budget dilemmas.It is easy to look at this picture, get depressed, and conclude that there is no meaningful way forward and the nation is destined to continue a long process of economic, social, and ecological decay.The challenge Gar Alperovitz offers — throughout his entire body of work, but most pointedly in his new, highly readable book, What Then Must We Do? — is to insist that recognizing the weakness of liberalism is not good reason to give up on progressive goals.Recognizing liberalism’s weakness is the first needed step toward developing a bolder politics with real policy substance that is capable both of addressing key problems and altering, over time, the underlying power dynamics of the American political and economic system.This is, clearly, a much taller order than simply electing or re-electing a candidate. But at this stage, the challenge is still primarily intellectual and conceptual: how to develop a new paradigm for meaningful change that takes us beyond traditional liberal strategies and their limitations, both substantively and politically.Alperovitz shows how the long-term negative trends toward extreme inequality, high economic insecurity, and a lopsided top-heavy politics are the predictable result of the American version of capitalism — a system that concentrates the ownership of wealth and the ability to shape the contours of the economy in relatively few hands. The traditional liberal remedy — progressive taxation of income and corporate profits in order to fund public goods and some measure of re distribution — is too weak to offset the far-reaching consequences of narrow control of wealth and capital by a tiny proportion of the population. This is especially true in the United States because of our extremely weak labor movement and long history of using racial and cultural antagonisms to divide and conquer the working-class majority.What then is to be done? Alperovitz’s answer is clear: the remedy for skewed ownership patterns is to create new forms of wealth that are democratic in nature. The traditional socialist vision of large-scale public ownership likely still has some part to play in certain industries, but for the most part, what Alperovitz has in mind are smaller-scale institutions organized in a variety of ways to benefit a variety of “mini-publics”: workers who own the firm they work in, neighborhoods that own part or all of a development corporation or an affordable housing development, cities that provide not only traditional utilities (water, energy) but also newfangled ones such as Internet access, while also engaging in other entrepreneurial activities.If liberalism is weak in America, it will seem to many counterintuitive to claim that a more radical political and economic program — focused on the control and ownership of wealth — is more plausible politically than yet another rebranding or repackaging of core liberal ideas. But that is exactly what Alperovitz argues, drawing on two key observations.First, as a matter of fact, innovative community ownership strategies are already taking place across the United States — in an astonishing variety of fields and forms. What Then Must We Do? provides an overview of many of these innovations, as well as links to more detailed information. The most exciting large-scale innovation is the Evergreen Cooperative network, which has launched cutting-edge green businesses, structured as cooperatives, in a working-class, high-poverty area of Cleveland, drawing on the buying power of existing urban institutions such as hospitals and universities, as well as on a variety of streams of public money. The long-term goal is to create an American version of the famed Mondragón system of industrial cooperatives in the Basque region of Spain.Second, localities and even states are likely to be driven increasingly toward community ownership strategies in the future because they need to find new secure revenue streams and new methods to stabilize jobs for the long term. A city-owned business or retail development that returns profit to city coffers can help stabilize municipal finances without resorting to unpopular tax increases. A worker-owned cooperative that receives modest public assistance is a more rational economic development strategy than a large subsidy to a major corporation, which is all too likely to move jobs to a higher bidder as soon as it gets a chance.Alperovitz’s claim that it might be possible not only to craft a fundamentally different progressive strategy but also to put the goal of system change on the table is certainly bold, but Alperovitz is also a realist. One of the key new concepts in this book is the notion of a “checkerboard strategy” — i.e., a political strategy that recognizes that while not all moves are available on all places on the board, there is always a move (maybe even a jump!) available somewhere: some way to put creative ownership-oriented strategies on the local policy agenda.Alperovitz concedes that there may be some places where the power dynamics or ideological winds don’t allow any movement or experimentation. But there are many places — especially the cities and counties that went for Barack Obama in the last two elections — where much is possible, as policymakers seek creative solutions to longstanding problems.Here there are two ways to see things. When one looks at what happens in Washington, and the way the Democratic Party compromises on issue after issue, and reflects on the power of corporate donors over prominent Democrats, one might reach the conclusion that the Democratic Party simply cannot be made a progressive vehicle. That judgment in fact is almost certainly true if one is thinking in terms of a “New New Deal” version of a vigorous national liberalism.But what if one is instead playing a checkerboard strategy and looking for places around the country to build meaningful, practical models of community ownership that both spread the wealth around and solve problems? In that case, what one will often encounter at the local level are sincere people (often Democrats or Independents, and sometimes Republicans) who ran for office because they wanted to help improve their communities, got elected, and now find that the resources just aren’t there to enact meaningful change. True, such folks might eventually get cynical, settle for enjoying the perks of power, and slowly forget why they entered politics in the first place. But before that happens, they may be surprisingly open to fresh new ideas — ideas that involve democratic forms of ownership. This is where the weakness of liberalism and the prolonged period of economic stagnation and fiscal strain combine to create a genuine political opportunity: an opportunity to get frustrated local leaders to pursue something genuinely different.In the long run, an ownership-based progressive agenda could reshape the power base of at least some cities and help form the foundation for a more powerful national progressive politics than faded New Deal–style liberalism.Here it’s important to understand that while Alperovitz shows that there is more room to move at the local level in the current political climate, just doing feel-good projects, let alone localism for localism’s sake, is not the point. The aim of local action is not just to create new democratic ownership structures but also to create new power bases in cities and localities that can serve as a credible alternative to the corporate-led regimes that prevail in the vast majority of American cities.There is also a still larger aim: to develop a multitude of credible, tested democratic ownership structures that can be the basis for a national movement and a genuine alternative to neoliberal economic paradigms. A national movement cannot subsist on Occupy-type resistance activities alone: it needs a positive agenda with many practical examples of how people-centered economic institutions can work.A serious effort to multiply alternative ownership models would also give progressive forces a tool that was entirely lacking in the 2008 economic crisis: a practical alternative program. To take just one example, the Obama bailout of General Motors focused on the narrow task of how to restore GM as a profitable company while saving some jobs along the way. An administration (or political movement) committed to democratic ownership might have used the takeover of GM as an opportunity to undergo a massive conversion away from a car-centered economy. Such an administration might have prioritized job stabilization and community stability, and it might have sought to maintain a permanent workers’ and public stake in the company to achieve those goals.To put it another way: no one has a perfect road map for how dramatic changes to the political-economic system might come about. But there is good reason to think capitalism will soon enough be in crisis mode, and there will be nasty right-wing responses seeking to exploit that moment. A coherent response from the Left requires not just bold ideas but also practical examples to point to. Attempts to build democratic ownership structures should not be conceived as merely local projects but as part of a larger movement whose aim is to forge a credible alternative to traditional forms of capitalism.So what is to be done right now? Read Alperovitz’s book, look at your local checkerboard, and find (or create) opportunities to get your local officials to consider trying to replicate one, two, or three of the dozens of community wealth innovations now underway — or even start a new one. Then connect with activists doing the same in other places and begin building the infrastructure for a sustained political movement focused squarely on democratizing wealth.That’s work enough for the decade ahead — and a far more productive way to spend one’s political energy than simply whining about Obama, the Democratic Party, or even the Tea Party.

title: The Long Goodbye
abstract: The Evergreen Theater on Poplar Avenue has gone by many names in its nearly one hundred years in the heart of Midtown Memphis: the Ritz Theater, the Guild Theater, Movie House on Poplar, and the Circuit Playhouse. As the Evergreen Theater, part of TheatreWorks Memphis, it hosts shows from local performance groups including Friends of George’s (a local LGBTQ+ company) and Cazateatro (a Spanish/English bilingual group). To Memphians, the Evergreen is perhaps best known for hosting a monthly showing of The Rocky Horror Picture Show. On Labor Day weekend of 2022, it was home to the world premiere of The Long Goodbye, an original musical theater experience conceived by Emily Rooker, the creator, director, and lead performer. While the show does not center any one religious tradition, the connection between the deceased and the living is a central theme of the show, interwoven with memory, grief, guilt, sadness, absence, fear, and many other themes that traditionally accompany presentations of death on stage. It is a public mourning of several important people in Rooker’s life, while also serving as an opportunity to dramatically and musically engage with the versions of herself that have been shaped by those losses.A rock opera in two acts, The Long Goodbye has minimal set decoration and relies mainly on the larger-than-life sounds of the six-piece rock band (situated upstage right) and the vibrant cast of local performers for its lasting impact. The actual plot is also minimal, since the emotional core of the songs leaves the possibility for varied interpretation by its audience members, but takes the audience on a journey of love, grief, and self-acceptance. Rooker, as “Self,” engages with her “Young Self” (Abby Frances) and her “Wicked Self” (Kristian Thomas), who are only named in the program, never called by those names on stage. She also interacts with performers credited as the “Mirrors,” the “Burden Dancers,” and the “Ballerina Ghosts.” Rooker, who is not part of an established theater group, found most of the performers through her own involvement in the Memphis songwriting and pole dancing communities; pole dancing is featured in the show’s second act.Rooker explains that all of the characters are in some way reflections or representations of the Self; the show is about reckoning with past versions of the Self and how we engage with them, grieve their loss, or revert to them. There is also a specific color palette assigned to each character to give them visual richness and establish their identities. However, beyond that, Rooker doesn’t want to be explicit with symbols or what they mean in order to allow the audience to engage with the Selves individually and draw meaning from their performance. In that way, the viewer can engage in private contemplation while witnessing a public spectacle of mourning and redemption.Women’s bodies are at the center of the show; the cast is entirely composed of female and nonbinary performers of a variety of racial backgrounds and body types. From the dancing to the costuming to the content of the songs themselves, female and non-binary bodies are celebrated in a way that does not conform to the objectification of the male gaze. There is a freedom and sensuality to the performance, but also an acknowledgement of how we hold grief, sadness, and trauma in our bodies and how we are conditioned to see our bodies as imperfect and undeserving of love. Rooker explains that the cast members exist in “bodies that are constantly politicized, policed, and whose genders are not taken seriously.” However, she admits that the exclusive casting of female and nonbinary performers was accidental; she primarily cast people she knew who expressed interest in the themes of the show. Intentional or not, the show is a celebration of women in all their complexity and the multitudes that they contain.The emotional progression of the rock opera develops through its seventeen songs, which were the original seed of the production. Rooker and her husband, Nate Smith, recorded the songs as an album in August 2020 almost entirely within their own home studio in Memphis. She had written the songs in 2017 and 2018 following the death of her aunt Annie in order to help process her grief and articulate her relationship with other family members who had passed away, such as her father and her grandfather. They were also crafted as she was going through many other life changes like marriage, therapy, and friends moving away, including her bandmates from local indie band Name and the Nouns. Rooker’s belting, mezzo-soprano voice almost entirely carries the show, and it does so with control and confidence. The other performers provide backing vocals and occasional harmonies; while they have no dialogue, they engage with the music in a variety of ways. They serve as characters within the stories that the songs are telling, and they dance, including pole dances, ballet-inspired movement, and an interpretative piece with butterfly wings by non-binary performer Mars McKay.While the individual songs deal with different themes, they form part of a coherent narrative, both as an album and as the visual rock opera that Rooker creates. Many of the songs start out small and intimate, and gradually explode into powerful anthems of love, grief, hope, sadness, and triumph, often within the same song. Act 1 opens with “Ghostlude 1,” which begins with the opening line, “I can still write a song down on the pages,” teaching the audience that her voice is in control of what they are about to see. It features “Burden” and “Waves,” exploring how the Self fits into a romantic relationship, while the brief “Alone” features instrumental riffs on the repeated lyrics “I can’t be alone.” Rooker explores family relationships in “When I Was Young,” which waxes nostalgic for childhood while acknowledging a complicated relationship with family members, whose deaths can revert us to a childlike state. The first act winds down with “So Many Times I’ve Disappeared,” a solemn reflective ballad about depression and anxiety, and ends with “B.K.T.Y.” (Be Kinder To Yourself), a six-minute journey of negative body image, harmful self-talk, the feeling that one is undeserving of love, and our tendency to see the worst in ourselves. Rooker engages with her “Young Self” and her “Wicked Self” as she moves from self-loathing to self-acceptance, and the emotions (ranging from fear and shame to compassion and love) are all visible on the faces of the Selves.Act 2 opens with “Sinking Feeling” and “DDC Reprise,” bringing the audience once again into a realm of depression, anxiety, and complicated feelings of grief. The standout song of the second act is “For Annie,” another six-minute journey, this time of Annie (an avatar of Rooker’s late aunt, played by Mars McKay) moving through a passageway flanked by all of the other performers before arriving into the arms of the Glam Reaper (Kate Peckham), a Death-like figure shrouded in sequins and sporting large platform heels. The departure of Annie from the Self’s world is the emotional core of the show, and Rooker takes care to send her off with love and elegance, perhaps the sort of elegance that the dying are not afforded in real life. As with the rest of the show, the music, lyrics, and staging appear to be a mixture of lament, farewell, redemption, eulogy, repentance, and tribute, all woven together in a tender performance that contains many of the sentiments that one would wish to convey to a loved one approaching death.“For Annie” functions as a microcosm of the whole production, as Rooker seems to move through an accelerated version of the stages of grief. Annie’s send-off begins with the Selves bargaining with Annie, trying to help her and heal her, and expressing lament that they cannot pull her back from the brink. Annie, who never speaks, is never able to tell us what her struggles were or what caused her death, but there is an implication that it was at least in part, her own decision based on her refusal to accept help. Rooker said that the first line of this song, “I do believe that love is never wasted,” is the first line that she wrote of this album/show. She then follows it with the lyrics “I only wish my love might have saved you / I wish it weren’t too late.” At the end of the song, the embrace of the Glam Reaper is the natural conclusion, and feels peaceful in spite of the emotional chaos left in its wake.The second act does not end with “For Annie,” however; there are five more songs, including the eerie “Ghostlude 2,” the angry “Mirror,” and the pessimistic “Warm Winter,” which all flow into each other and contain multitudes. The penultimate song of the second act, “Water the Earth,” paints a picture of the cyclical nature of life and death while acknowledging the suffering in between. Just after proclaiming in “Warm Winter” that Death has followed her all of her life, Rooker anticipates her own eventual death, both the end of her own suffering and her ability to grow flowers from her own decomposing body. The dance between the nihilistic line “How do you remember, I want to forget” and the optimistic “Let it be simple, let something grow” is emblematic of Rooker’s ability to see a situation from multiple perspectives and come to different conclusions simultaneously. Finally, the second act concludes with the triumphant “I’m Still Here,” an optimistic anthem to resilience, self-love, healing, and overcoming adversity. The entire cast dances together on stage, including Annie with her butterfly wings, and the audience is left with hope and a sense of liberation.All of the songs are anchored by Rooker’s strong voice, passionate performance, and personal connection to the material. The Long Goodbye might feel a bit familiar to those who enjoy performance art, rock opera, and Rooker’s own history of songwriting, but it stands on its own as a personal testimonial and musical exploration of loss. The style of the music is not derivative, but Rooker herself has cited a range of influences including Pink Floyd, the Arctic Monkeys, Fleetwood Mac, Young Dolph, and Lucy Dacus. Specific songs that Rooker credits include “Death with Dignity’ by Sufjan Stevens (in terms of instrumentation) and “Hurt” by Nine Inch Nails (in terms of tone). When designing the scene in which Annie departs, she also took inspiration from the scene in Rent in which Angel dies and all of the characters line up to wish him farewell.Perhaps because it was independently produced, The Long Goodbye did not receive a lot of local press attention; it was funded via Kickstarter and both sold-out shows were populated largely through word of mouth. The album is available for streaming on Spotify and YouTube, and there was an encore production at the Evergreen Theater in January of 2023. Audience reaction has been positive; Rooker had a friend who saw the show twice and nicknamed it “The Long Good Cry,” which is her favorite review. The show allows its audience to feel, process, and engage with heavy feelings of grief, hurt, and loss that many people are carrying around with them, particularly in the wake of a deadly pandemic, but are forced to ignore for the majority of the day just to get through it. There is an intimate connection with the audience, particularly in a small theater like the Evergreen, which allowed the performers to feel the audience’s reaction viscerally.The Long Goodbye is a powerful, cathartic, and expressive reflection on death: its inevitability, its impact on those left behind, and how the relationship with the departed can continue in our memories, our art, and our bodies. Rooker never tells the audience how to feel or how to grieve their own losses, but her own specific presentation of her personal grief makes the public spectacle of mourning feel highly relevant to anyone who has experienced loss. Meanwhile, there is a deeply intimate undercurrent of the Self and how one engages in self-love, self-loathing, self-criticism, and hopefully, eventually, self-acceptance; Rooker celebrates the female body while acknowledging that women are often prone to hate their own bodies and that self-acceptance is something that must be practiced. While The Long Goodbye deals with dark themes and shines a light on negative thoughts and traumatizing experiences, the ultimate message is that we are deserving of love, even after we are gone. In the wake of loss, personal grief and public mourning are a manifestation of that love, and at the end of a life, one could only hope to be remembered with a musical theater legacy such as this.

title: Menstrual Disorders
abstract: After reading this article, readers should be able to:The onset of menstruation in young women is a milestone with personal, cultural, and medical ramifications. Menarche heralds the onset of fertility, which can be cause for both celebration and trepidation for the patient, her family, and clinicians. It behooves both general and specialist pediatricians to be comfortable discussing what is normal and what is not normal about menstruation. Young women who have special health-care needs and their families deserve particular attention. Both the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists encourage pediatricians to think of menstruation as a “vital sign” for women. (1)(2) Irregular, absent, or overly painful periods should be evaluated, closely monitored, and managed proactively.In both the evaluation and treatment of menstrual disorders, it is critical to keep in mind the patient’s perspective on her symptoms. It is extremely valuable to hear from the patient what her expectations of menses are, and where she has derived these expectations. In conditions ranging from polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) to endometriosis, the patient’s quality of life has been shown to be much more strongly linked to her own perception of her symptoms than to her doctors’ assessment of their severity. Periods perceived as heavy, painful, or abnormal can be a significant cause of school absence and decreased work productivity. What many patients and families desire as much as relief from menses or menstrual pain is predictability. Setting realistic expectations from the onset of medical treatment goes a long way in improving quality of life.The presence of menses can be a challenge to the families of young women who have special health-care needs, and particular sensitivity is warranted. The onset of menstruation may raise what can be uncomfortable questions about fertility and sexual activity (voluntary or otherwise) for the families of these young women. Patients and families appreciate and deserve the opportunity to talk openly about these subjects.The median age of menarche in the United States is 12.4 years, with African-American girls experiencing menarche slightly earlier on average than non-Hispanic white and Mexican-American girls, as determined in the third National Health and Nutrition Evaluation Survey. (3) The usual sequence of events leading up to menarche includes thelarche (Tanner [sexual maturation rating] stage 2 breast development) at a median age of 10.2 years and pubarche (Tanner stage 2 pubic hair) at a median age of 11.6 years, but recent studies have revealed that girls are developing breasts and pubic hair earlier than in past generations although the age of menarche has remained more constant. (4) Some girls, particularly African-American girls, may experience pubarche before thelarche. Early pubarche, especially accompanied by obesity and insulin resistance, is associated with later development of PCOS.The definition of precocious puberty remains controversial because of mixed data about how ethnicity and adiposity affect development. Generally, the presence of breast development or pubic hair before age 8 years is considered precocious, although girls whose BMI is greater than 85% or who are African-American or Mexican-American may have earlier development. In one study, 27% of African-American girls had signs of pubertal development at age 7 years, compared with 7% of white girls. (5) Menarche occurring after age 14.1 years occurs in only 5% of girls in the United States; the definition of primary amenorrhea is failure to achieve menarche by age 15 years. Failure to progress from thelarche to menarche within 3 years is also cause for concern.It was thought previously that hypothalamic axis immaturity in the first gynecologic year was common, and therefore menstrual irregularity was to be expected. More current data indicate that even in the first gynecologic year, amenorrhea for more than 3 months is uncommon in healthy girls in the United States and should be investigated if there are other issues apparent, or if the pattern persists into the second year. A normal menstrual cycle (counting from the first day of one menstrual period to the first day of menses of the next cycle) is 21 to 35 days in adults but has a slightly wider range of normal in adolescents during the first 2 years after menarche. A normal period lasts from 3 to 7 days. Bleeding lasting 8 or more days is considered prolonged.The menstrual cycle is divided commonly into three phases: follicular (proliferative), ovulation, and luteal (secretory) (Figure). The follicular phase may vary in length, but the luteal phase is 14 days during normal ovulatory cycles. Ovulation is the event that defines regular cycles and triggers the prostaglandin cascade, which is associated with primary dysmenorrhea.Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) secretion in the hypothalamus is pulsatile and stimulates the pituitary gland to secrete luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), which stimulates follicle growth in the ovary. A dominant follicle in the ovary secretes increasing amounts of estrogen, which causes the endometrial lining to proliferate. A feedback loop develops in which increasing amounts of estrogen result in decreasing LH and FSH levels; but above a certain estrogen level, the negative feedback is reversed and LH release from the pituitary is stimulated. This “LH surge” triggers ovulation.After ovulation, the remaining follicular cells in the ovary luteinize and become the corpus luteum. This corpus luteum secretes estrogen and progesterone, which has the effect of stabilizing the endometrium and causing differentiation into glandular tissue to produce the spongy lining needed for implantation of a fertilized ovum. If fertilization and implantation do not occur, human chorionic gonadotropin is not produced, and the corpus luteum involutes. The withdrawal of progesterone (and estrogen) levels derived from the corpus luteum is the trigger for the shedding of the endometrial lining, or menses. In anovulatory girls, menstrual periods occur from a proliferative endometrium because of waxing and waning of estrogen levels.Primary amenorrhea is clinically defined as the lack of menses by the age of 15 years or by more than 3 years after the onset of secondary sexual development. Lack of any secondary sexual characteristics by age 13 years also is abnormal and should be investigated. Secondary amenorrhea is defined as 3 months of amenorrhea after the achievement of menarche. Underlying conditions may overlap in primary and secondary amenorrhea (Table 1). Careful history and physical examination are crucial to diagnosis. It cannot be overstated, however, that a sensitive pregnancy test must be part of the initial evaluation of any patient with amenorrhea, regardless of the reported sexual history. Besides pregnancy, disordered eating patterns and weight changes are among the most common reasons for amenorrhea. Review of a growth chart is important in considering the possible causes.The differential diagnosis of primary amenorrhea includes genital tract abnormalities, as well as endocrine causes (which also may cause secondary amenorrhea), including hypothalamic/pituitary, ovarian, thyroid, or adrenal abnormalities. The assessment of the patient should include a detailed history and physical examination, laboratory testing, and radiologic imaging in some cases.The patient and parent should be asked about a past medical history of chronic illness, tempo of any pubertal development, weight gain or loss, exercise habits, and stressors. Family history should focus on any potential endocrine disorders in first-order relatives, including thyroid disease, diabetes, PCOS, and infertility. The parent should be asked also about any family history of constitutional delay of menses. Sexual history should be obtained confidentially, because pregnancy is a rare but possible cause of primary amenorrhea and the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea.Social stressors may contribute to primary or secondary amenorrhea, and asking about academic pressure, family conflict, mood disorders, body image, and eating behaviors is important. Clinicians should ask about history of medication use, including any antipsychotic medication, contraceptive use (adolescents often forget or deny use unless asked specifically), and illicit drug use. The review of systems should include discussion of acne or unwanted hair growth, weight changes, mood changes, disordered eating attitudes and behavior, change in bowel habits, abdominal pain, headaches, visual changes, galactorrhea, and vaginal discharge.The review of a growth chart identifies patients who are overweight or underweight for height. Girls who are overweight for height and not growing appropriately are more likely to have an endocrinopathy (hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome), whereas patients underweight for height may have a deficit of calories (eating disorder or bowel disease such as inflammatory bowel disease or celiac disease).The patient who has exceptionally short stature (final height predicted to be less than 5 ft in the patient who has normal parental heights), with or without other features such as webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, shield chest, and high arched palate, and primary amenorrhea raises concerns about Turner syndrome (45,X) or mosaicism (46,XX/45,X). Consultation with a geneticist or endocrinologist may be warranted.Physical examination should include assessment of height, weight, and BMI in addition to routine vital signs. The clinician should examine the patient’s skin thoroughly. Peripheral visual fields should be checked by confrontation and the fundi examined. The clinician should test for, or at least ask about, the presence of smell (anosmia is associated with Kallmann syndrome). The thyroid gland should be palpated for enlargement. Tanner staging should be recorded and tracked over time, and breast examination should verify whether there is any galactorrhea. Abdominal palpation should be performed to detect constipation or the presence of any masses.An external genital evaluation should be performed to detect clitoromegaly (clitoral glans wider than 0.5 cm) and patency of the introitus. All that is necessary for an internal examination in virginal patients may be passage of a saline moistened cotton-tip swab to assess the depth of the vagina (7–8 cm is average for a postpubertal young woman). If there is any question of an anatomic abnormality, pelvic ultrasonography should be performed at a center experienced with prepubertal patients.The range of congenital abnormalities includes external anomalies such as imperforate hymen and transverse vaginal septum with normal müllerian structures, as well as müllerian anomalies such as uterine and vaginal agenesis. Appropriate and consistent visual examination of the vaginal introitus in the newborn and at health maintenance visits should prevent the late diagnosis of imperforate hymen. Early detection can help avoid the “classic” presentation of imperforate hymen in a postpubertal young woman: cyclic abdominal pain, midline abdominal mass, and purplish bulging seen at the introitus of the vagina (a hematocolpos, which may be remarkably large). title: Traversing the Limits of the Ecological Elegy
abstract: The elegiac mode looms large in literary explorations of ecological grief, that grief which is “felt in relation to experienced or anticipated ecological losses due to acute or chronic environmental change” (Cunsolo and Ellis 275). Loosely defined as “a lyric, usually formal in tone and diction, suggested either by the death of an actual person or by the poet’s contemplation of the tragic aspects of life” (Fogle 62), the elegy has emerged since the mid-seventeenth century as the dominant conduit for mourning in Anglophone poetries. Within this period, the ecological violence instated by European colonial-capitalism has continued unabated. Ecosystems across the earth have been beset by “double death,” death that leads to more death, as the death of one being takes away what another needs to survive (Rose).1 When double death occurs, multispecies communities lose not only beloved individuals but also knowledge, infrastructure, lifeways, and entire generations of the as-yet-unborn. In its encounters with double death, elegy is met by particular resonances and challenges, alongside a growing body of scholarly discourse. Given the breadth of US poetry associated with ecological elegy,2 Marcella Durand has good reason to suggest that ecopoetics might itself “be becoming a form of elegy.”3 Margaret Ronda and Bonnie Costello trace a strand of “eco-elegy” through the work of W. S. Merwin, Jorie Graham, Ed Roberson, Maxine Kumin, Amy Clampitt, and many others (Ronda 95; Costello 334–38). That the ecological elegy’s relevance endures into the twenty-first century is clear (Schell 156), as is its capacity to evolve in response to inherited structural expectations (Ronda 97), in line with the tradition of anti-elegy.4 So tenacious is the ecological elegy, in fact, that it is frequently invoked in the titles of artworks of all kinds.5 And yet, the ecological elegy’s dominant position in environmentally conscious art does not mean that it is without limits and limitations, nor that there cannot be an ecopoetics, or simply a poetics, of ecological grief that lies beyond such limits. The idea that more attention ought to be paid to the limits of ecological elegy is not a new one, though its proponents tend to focus on ontological or ethical limitations, which are often predicated upon imprecise characterizations of the mode. Durand asks whether there is “an ecopoetics elegy large enough to grieve for an entire system,” but elegy’s foundational sense of insufficiency is, as I demonstrate, not prohibitive to its efforts to engage ecological grief. Meanwhile, Timothy Morton contends that the ecological elegy will “wither or mutate” at some undetermined point in the future because it is “about burying the dead,” an impossible and ethically dubious task where the double death of ecosystemic breakdown is concerned (104–5). Morton’s reading here elides how elegy has always been complicated by the impossibility of burying grief, even before Jahan Ramazani’s observation that modern elegy tends “not to heal but to reopen the wounds of loss” (Ramazani xi). As much as the elegist may wish to “do the mourning for you” in “the grief equivalent of canned laughter” (Morton 105), this impulse can be frustrated in even the most conventional and canonical of elegies, including that pinnacle of Victorian public elegy, Alfred Tennyson’s In Memoriam A. H. H. (Gray 274). Morton’s prediction about the demise of elegy relies upon an oversimplification of its aims, coupled with the assumption that morally reprehensible forms will always be superseded. However, he also gestures toward an insoluble truth: elegy is not synonymous with poetry about loss. One can choose how one writes, reads, and thinks about ecological grief, and one need not choose elegy, because the mode has definitional limits. Though elegy’s significance has shifted many times (including a stint as a form of erotic love poetry), it remains a mode of European origins with several millennia of convoluted history. It is therefore inherently partial, beholden, if at times only antagonistically, to the legacy that it perpetuates, as well as to the funerary beliefs and customs alongside which it has developed.6 In this article, I examine the partiality of elegy and, by extension, the partiality of its ecological iterations. Some scholars extend elegy to describe an ever-greater range of texts: most persuasively, Arnold Krupat theorizes a “Native American elegiac expression” distinct from “Western elegy.” Meanwhile, I argue that there is space as well for a more circumscribed understanding of elegy.7 Such an understanding allows one to attend both to the specific complexities that elegy is able to sustain and to the possibilities unleashed by works that dwell around and beyond its bounds. A narrower definition makes possible more nuanced ways of reading, adding to rather than subtracting from the ambiguities that make elegy such a rich source of study. Fogle provides a useful point of departure, but if all formal lyrics that contemplate “the tragic aspects of life” were elegies, the mode would be ubiquitous to the point of meaninglessness. I begin by drawing on Wendell Berry’s “The Peace of Wild Things” (1968) to suggest that elegy is troubled by a series of fragile cycles, structured around the return of an obscured beloved, the possibility of consolation, and the impulse to publicly articulate grief. Ecological elegy grieves ruptures in ecosystemic relationality, often attempting to tesselate its fragile cycles with the straight line of apocalypse narrative. Ecological elegy is challenged by the instability that is produced by these attempts, but it is not entirely undone by them. Where ecological elegy can falter is in the positioning of its speaker, who generally grieves for the lost other, not with them. Though they may care deeply about the loss, they care from a position of distance that confers a sense of relative security. They may survive the other’s experience of apocalyptic world-ending. Perhaps, then, grieving with presents is one way of moving beyond elegy. In the final part of this article, I turn to C. D. Wright’s “Song of the Gourd” (1992) and Linda Hogan’s “Bones at the River” (2020), to demonstrate how both writers at times pull away from elegy’s fragile cycles, the imposition of the apocalypse narrative, and the associated tendency to grieve for. These poems grieve not for but with, in a position of entanglement that necessitates personal risk. I propose that these works are constitutive of a poetics of ecological grief, an assemblage of creative work that explores poesis, making, as a means of grieving ruptures in ecosystemic relationality brought about by double death. This poetics of ecological grief may not always lie entirely beyond elegy, but it is not governed by the mode’s inherited expectations. Neither is this poetics inherently contemporary, of course. I draw here upon contemporary examples to emphasize that the recent proliferation of scholarly interest in ecological elegy sits alongside work that transcends ecological-elegiac writing.8 What the poetics of ecological grief provides is a theorization of literary expressions of ecological grief that does not universalize a mode of European origin. In cleaving exclusively to elegy, one risks not only losing its specificity as a critical term but also narrowing an understanding of ecological grief just when humans need to address its pluralities and asymmetries. Ecological losses are unevenly distributed across global communities in ways that require one to think critically about the kinds of ecological grief that are foregrounded in public discourse. Who is able and allowed to grieve? What sorts of states or practices are recognized as grief? In the words of Malcom Ferdinand, a “double fracture […] separates the colonial history of the world from its environmental history,” as environmental policies, practices, and discourses continue to deny and reinforce the colonial causes of the contemporary climate crisis (3). Might elegy’s prominent position in ecocritical discourse be a product of the double fracture that Ferdinand names, indicative of a Eurocentric approach to reading and organizing texts about environmental loss? title: Desire in Chromatic Harmony: A Psychodynamic Exploration of Fin de Siècle Tonality
abstract: Drawing from the union of psyche and music as its formative datum, Desire in Chromatic Harmony takes a unique approach from the start. Revolving around the libidinal concept of desire, Kenneth M. Smith brings music theory into dialogue with psychodynamics—the branch of psychoanalysis and philosophy in the Freudian tradition—in an effort to account for the psychological faculties of post-Wagnerian tonal music in a novel theory of chromatic harmony. To this end, he turns to the psychodynamic means of Jacques Lacan, supplemented by the works of Sigmund Freud, Gilles Deleuze, and Jean-François Lyotard, among others, to create an integrative musico-psychological framework that informs both the music-theoretical formulation of desire and the philosophical discussions of chromatic chord progressions. The foundation of such a model and its dependent music-theoretical apparatus are established in the extensive first chapter, where psychodynamics is deployed to reconcile the ostensibly discordant lines of thought in theories of chromatic tonality.Though acknowledging the possible structural role of chromaticism, Smith asserts that “our experience of fin de siècle harmony . . . is fundamentally diatonic” (ix) and patently gives diatonicism the epistemic priority in his tonal system. Considering diatonic logic as the regulative schema in fin-de-siècle tonality, the author naturally rests his new theory on the three primary tonal functions proposed initially by Hugo Riemann: tonic (T), subdominant (S), and dominant (D). Conceived as what Deleuze might call a triangular “Oedipal” structure, these diatonic pillars are reanimated with the psycholinguistic concepts of metaphor and metonymy, through which their functional mechanism is overhauled in light of the extended chromatic environment.For Smith, as for Lacan, metaphor and metonymy—like the British detective duo Holmes and Watson—depend on each other to operate in the unconscious working of desire, which is structured as a linguistic system of signifiers comparable to music. According to this conception, metaphor refers to the substitution of one signifier for another, and metonymy deals with the connection between signifiers. Metaphor suggests an attempt to reach a signified that cannot be completely reached (e.g., using words to describe feelings), a phenomenon that Smith finds in chord substitutions that deputize for the same function. Construing tonal functions as main carriers of musical meaning, Smith proposes that all chromatic chords are reducible to the three primary functions, and that chords can metaphorically represent these functions even if they bear only limited resemblance to the harmonic content of the latter. Such a possibility is indeed implied in the theoretical labyrinth of Ernö Lendvai (1993), whose axis system, reappraised through the ideas of Lacan, Brian Hyer, and others, offers the basis for Smith's metaphoric harmonic substitutions.Lendvai's system is predicated on the premise that tonality is marked by a “black hole” (66), a central lack which, understood from a Lacanian perspective, is covered by the master signifiers around which other signifiers are organized.1 His axis thus revolves around the three primary functions as the master signifiers that marshal substitutions based on minor-third relations. While relative major/minor relationships stand for the same function, the relative major and minor of the parallel relation are also functionally equivalent, because parallel relations are too similar to acquire different meanings.2 Joining the available substitutions together, this effectively produces three closed octatonic cycles corresponding to the three primary tonal functions, as presented in Figure 1, where chords a tritone apart are linked by their shared tritone when injected with their sevenths (as per the common post-Wagnerian harmonic practices). Functional substitutions are indicated by an upward or a downward arrow in accordance with the direction of their operation (e.g., in the key of C, A is the lower relative and is hence denoted by T↓), or by an asterisk (✦) in case of tritone swap.Having finessed chromatic tonal functionality with metaphoric substitution, Smith then illuminates the connection between functions via the notion of metonymy. Central to his conception of chord progression is the idea of discharge. Smith posits that the discharge of basic (or idealized) root motion is “as significant to functional interaction” as Daniel Harrison's (1994: 8) two classes of leading notes (7^–1^ in major and ♭6^–(5 in minor). The author hence calls attention to the discharge action of rooted chords as a whole—which he indicates by the italicized discharge and directed arrows (→ and ←)—as fundamental to the succession of functions: TdischargesD and accumulates tension toward S; DdischargesS and reinforces the desire for T; and S stands in the middle, both as “an ‘other’ region of relative stability” to T and as “an auxiliary store of tension” discharging into D (8). Since in a single octatonic cycle none of the chords possesses the leading tones of the other, neither discharge nor discharge is possible between chords associated with the same function. Consequently, an octatonic collection is said to store up functional energy that allows it to be discharged to another, with each shift involving a functional discharge.Although such functional discharges would make up the familiar T→S → D→T progression, they are to be construed as a form of Lacanian metonymy, which concerns “the connection between signifiers and the perpetual sliding of one signifier beneath another” (33). According to Smith, the metonymic process interrupts metaphoric signification and creates constant connections of new signifiers, moving further away from the signified and in turn generating desire that is, in Lacan's ([1966] 2006: 431) words, “caught in the rails of metonymy, eternally extending towards the desire for something else.” In musical terms, functional metonymy yields “an indefinite chain of equal-tempered fifth relations and a microfunctional T→S → D rotation” (34) that enables the functions and their metaphoric substitutes to be strung together. As tonal functions are roped, they serve as not only vessels of tension but also sites of functional discharge and therefore meaning. This double role renders functional meaning “forever elided”: while metonym gives voice to metaphor by activating functional expression, metaphor “is always asserted retroactively back along the metonymic axis,” because “we cannot label a chord T until we have heard its musical phrase and experienced the function-sealing cadence” (37). In short, in Smith's tonal universe, functional interpretations are open to subsequent reevaluation, and “there is a constant slippage between chords and functions, arrested only at certain points of a musical phrase” (37), or what Lacan would call point de capiton, with which the sense of meaning emerges.Smith next treats this metaphoric-metonymic functional paradigm with a series of theoretical refinements and philosophical explorations in case studies spanning from Wagner to Aaron Copland. Consistent with the elected approach, music theory and psychodynamics continue to intertwine in concept making. While the overall discourse loosely follows a historical thread in the study of libidinal desire, the first half of the book is mainly devoted to the expansion of the neofunctional system. After establishing root motion as the basis of triadic transactions, Smith attends to the issue of seventh chords through the romantic provenance of psychodynamic music. He contends that chromatic seventh chords often express two separate functions, with its immediate constituents conveying mostly D and its syntactic position articulating either S or T, and that similar tension chords such as augmented and diminished triads can also project any of the three functions depending on the context.The metonymic slippage of these multivalent chords is examined in light of the quintessential Vorspiel and Liebestod from Tristan und Isolde, where functions are elucidated as necessary Lacanian phantasies that “create the signifying chain in which harmonic desire can persist” (79). As the cyclicity of the T→S → D→Tdischarging units displays teleonomy, the author proceeds to relate such repetitions to the concept of cybernetics, self-regulatory mechanisms operating through circular and repeated feedback loops. He argues that they enact and renew functional experience at different hierarchical levels that can in turn afford modulation, as exemplified in the works of Charles Ives and Copland. In view of the manifold discharge possibilities that polychords can invoke in each cybernetic cycle, an investigation of how these harmonic “drives” behave follows.3 With reference to Deleuze and Guattari's universalizing triune “daddy–mommy–me” (Deleuze and Guattari [1972] 2004: 87), Smith declares that harmonic drives are frequently suppressed by a similar Oedipal structure of tonal functions (D, S, T), a desiring matrix that we should aim to get past. Parsing Karol Szymanowski's harmonic language, he thereby develops a method called drive analysis, which mobilizes triangles and squares with different corner shapes to represent triads, tetrachords, and their chromatic alterations on a grid: the grid captures the multiplicity of simultaneous drives and the discharge path, wherein the drive, per Lacan, deconstructs its object by merely perpetuating its aim without pondering its goal.4The meticulous theoretical work subsequently paves the way for the philosophical ruminations of psychodramatic music in the second half of the book. Central to this musico-psychological inspection is the idea of functional rotation as the engine that motivates psychodramas. Beginning with Richard Strauss's Elektra, Smith traces the dependent relationship between Elektra and Agamemnon in the functional rotations of the opera and repudiates the common hysteric reading of Elektra via the concept of perversion. By appealing to the Lacanian pervert, Smith spotlights the ways in which Elektra correlates her harmonic gaze with that of Agamemnon and allows the latter to speak through her; this gives Elektra the feeling that she is in control of the gaze, and in turn she becomes the object of Agamemnon's drive. While the opera closes by breaking down the desiring functional circuit as a form of cure for Elektra, it also points to her other persona as a Deleuzian schizophrenic whose desire to create connections with “a multiplicity of ‘becomings’” is now countered by her final disconnection from desiring production (230).5 As Deleuze takes the stage, the cybernetic nature of repetition is brought to the fore for further examination. Considering the phenomenon of pitch-tethering, Smith contends that a Deleuzian model of difference—articulated through repetition—is at play in parsimonious voice-leading as “desire's guiding principle,” in lieu of the Hegelian-Lacanian dialectic seen in the T–D antagonism (239).6Since the tethering pitch is established by way of repetition and recurrence, Smith then proposes nine levels of cyclical cybernetic repetition inspired by Deleuze, elevating from the material spaces of pitch, chord, key, piece, and intra-opus to more conceptual spaces of inter-opus, contemporary composition, life, and philosophy—the processes of which, as Smith skillfully demonstrates, can be elucidated through the Tonnetz. Apposite to Josef Suk's compositional technique, these repetitions are interpreted in dialogue with Freud's concept of death drive, through which Smith offers a psychoanalytic reading of recurring tropes in Suk's music including melancholia, mourning, and mother.The different strands of music-theoretical and psychodynamic thoughts ultimately converge in a concluding study of Alexander Skryabin's Piano Sonata No. 10, op. 70. In light of Deleuze's remarks about cybernetics and acceleration, Smith probes how tonal desire flows through octatonic and hexatonic spaces by perusing Skryabin's “accelerationist” tendencies in his treatment of harmony and form.7 Combining the efforts of neo-functional theory, drive analysis, and the new Formenlehre, the author suggests that the work affords multiple mechanical processes, where the hastened global T→S → D→T progression is shown to “refract” through octatonicism and hexatonicism at different speeds as the thematic material generates formal rotations cybernetically (300). This refraction in turn attests to the accelerative and cybernetic nature of the sonata's economy of desire—a capitalist construction that, in Smith's closing words, made Skryabin “a most productive pioneer” (301).8Smith's model addresses a number of analytical problems pertinent to chromatic harmony—above all, the issue of tonicity. By redressing tonal functions as mental categories to which chords subscribe in context, he demonstrates that the concept of tonality does not necessarily hinge on the material manifestation of pitch orientation but rather can operate as an implied existence around which listening experience organizes. This abstract understanding effectively extends the definition of tonic fundamental to any claim of tonality: as Steven Rings (2019: 109) asserts, a tonic is characterized by “(a) a focal pitch class (b) with respect to which all remaining pitch classes in some musical passage are hierarchically arranged and perceived (c) even in its acoustic absence.” While tonic centricity might be a debatable notion for music at the turn of the twentieth century, Smith's tonal functions allow the tonic, in its absence, to be stood in by its metaphoric substitutes as the focal representation with reference to which the other pitch classes—deriving their meaning too by dint of tonal association—are hierarchically ordered and apprehended.9 Engaging and yet differing from neo-Riemannian theories where the tonic tends to be heard locally and assumed a priori, Smith's focal pitch class arises gradually through metonymic processes instead, leaving its supposed status as the center of gravity mostly a desired condition on an overarching level.10 In such a way, tonality continues to strive on its edge as a totalizing concept in the chromatic (and to an extent, post-tonal) pitch space, haunting our cognitive facilities of harmonic sense-making as sonic memories of diatonic structure remain in the unconscious.This treatment of tonal functions as bearers of harmonic meaning proves wide applicability, for Smith has convincingly attuned his neo-functional approach to music shaped by a great variety of and philosophical from to the fin de such Smith is to the of his theories to music. title: Free and Forgetful Come in Pairs ── A Roll Call of Adjunctions: Counting Hom Sets Checks the Correspondence, and One of Two Compactifications Is Not Even a Functor ── [Paper 246]
abstract: Operations that add something and operations that throw something away appear again and again: free constructions, completions, localisations, compactifications. These come in pairs, except that not all of them do. Under the single word compactification stood a left adjoint and something that is not even a functor. No new mathematical theorem and no new law is claimed. Scope of this paper (scope note): no new mathematical theorem and no new law is claimed. That free functors are left adjoint to forgetful ones, that the Stone-Cech compactification is a left adjoint, that the one-point compactification is functorial only for proper maps, and that the algebraic closure has no universal property are all standard. No measured value is cited; every number is obtained by exhaustive enumeration. No general category theory is developed; only the definition of an adjunction is used and the adjoint functor theorem is not entered. No point-set topology is developed; one instance of a map that fails to extend is used. The axiom of choice is not discussed; existence is separated from uniqueness and nothing more. No ranking of value is attached to being an adjoint; it is not claimed that a construction without an adjoint is inferior. The relation to earlier papers. Paper 153 separated three stages of forgetting and exhibited evidence that a right adjoint is absent; this paper counts the paired side, the left adjoints. Paper 201 showed that complete is four different claims; Section 5 separates which of them carries an adjoint. Paper 113 showed that a module is a limit rather than a wall, the neighbouring notion on the same shelf. Paper 149 treated the functoriality of pullback and pushforward; this paper looks at when such a functor has a partner. Paper 179 showed that cannot be constructed has several roots; Section 6 is a fourth case, existing but not unique. The setting. Two operations are adjoint when, roughly, maps out of the object built by one correspond one to one with maps into the object left by the other. The shape is that an operation which adds something is paired with an operation which throws something away. This paper names the constructions that are not paired. First, the pairing can be checked with numbers. Homomorphisms from the free group on n generators into a group must number exactly the order raised to the n, since the adjunction turns that into choosing n elements freely. For the cyclic group of order six and the symmetric group on three letters the counts at n equal to one, two and three are 6, 36 and 216. For the dihedral group of order eight and the quaternion group they are 8, 64 and 512. The count does not depend on the structure at all; one group is commutative and the other is not, and both give 216. Seen from a free group the interior of the target is invisible and only the number of elements shows. Second, a non-free source gives no power. Counting homomorphisms from a cyclic group, that is the elements whose n-th power is the identity, gives six for the dihedral group and two for the quaternion group at n equal to two. Neither is a power of eight, and now the interior of the target does show: two groups of the same order returned different numbers. Here is the separator. A cyclic group is not free; it imposes a relation, and to the extent that a relation is imposed the structure of the target enters the answer. Free means carrying no relation at all. Third, this is the core of the paper. Embedding a space into a closed one is called compactification, and there are two. The one-point compactification adds a single point at infinity, turning the line into a circle. The Stone-Cech compactification adds as much as possible. Take the plain inclusion of an open interval into the line and ask whether it extends to the one-point compactifications. It does not. The point at infinity of the interval is approached from both ends, while the inclusion sends those two ends to interior points of the line, where the point at infinity of the line is not. One point would need two destinations. The one-point compactification is therefore not even a functor on continuous maps, and becomes one only when restricted to proper maps: before any question of adjointness the correspondence fails to carry maps. The Stone-Cech construction, by contrast, is a left adjoint. Fourth, completion is not an adjoint until the class of maps is fixed. The completion of a metric space is an adjoint for uniformly continuous maps and for Lipschitz maps, and is not one for merely continuous maps. The reason is simple: a continuous map need not send Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences, so there is nothing to extend it to, and uniform continuity is placed there precisely to guarantee that. Writing that completion is a free construction requires saying which category. Fifth, the algebraic closure is not an adjoint. Every field has one, and it has the same shape as a completion: add what is missing and close up. Yet no universal property holds, and a map out of it into an algebraically closed field is not unique. The algebraic closure of the rationals carries infinitely many automorphisms other than the identity. It exists and is not unique. Paper 179 separated three roots of cannot be constructed, and this is a fourth case: constructible, but with no canonical construction. Failing to be an adjoint is not a defect and the algebraic closure is a perfectly useful construction; what is said here is only that the single phrase free construction erases this difference. Closing. Constructions that add something split into three stages: those that do not carry maps, those that carry maps without a partner, and those that have one. The separator is likewise three-fold. Does it carry maps at all? If so, does it have a partner? If so, in which category? Free construction, completion and closure all look alike and differ in whether a partner exists. Whether one exists can be seen by counting Hom sets: whether the count is the order raised to a power, and nothing more. On the making of this work: The ideas and content of this work stem from the author's own considerations. Assistance from an AI (a large language model) was used for structuring, English translation, and checking the algebra. Any remaining errors or misinterpretations are solely the author's. Feedback and corrections are sincerely appreciated. ----- 体系には「余計なものを足す」操作と「捨てる」操作が何度も現れる——自由化、完備化、局所化、コンパクト化。これらは対になっている。ただし全部が対になっているわけではない。同じ「コンパクト化」という語の下に、左随伴であるものと、関手ですらないものが並んでいた。新しい数学定理も新しい法則も主張しない。 本稿の射程(射程注記):新しい数学定理も新しい法則も主張しない。自由関手が忘却関手の左随伴であること、ストーン=チェックのコンパクト化が左随伴であること、一点コンパクト化が固有写像に対してのみ関手的であること、代数的閉包が普遍性を持たないことは、いずれも標準的である。測定値を引かない——本稿の数はすべて全数え上げで得たものである。圏論の一般論を作らない——随伴の定義だけを使い、随伴関手定理には立ち入らない。位相空間論を論じない——使うのは延長できない写像の実例ひとつである。選択公理を論じない——存在と一意性を分けるだけである。「随伴であること」に価値の順序をつけない——随伴でない構成が劣っているとは主張しない。 既刊との関係。論文153 は忘却関手を三段に分け、右随伴が無いことの証拠を挙げた——本稿はその対になる側、すなわち左随伴のほうを数える。論文201 は「完備」が四つの別の主張だと示した——第5節はそのうちどれが随伴を持つかを分ける。論文113 は「モジュールは壁ではなく、極限である」と示した——同じ圏論の棚の、隣の概念である。論文149 は引き戻しと押し出しの関手性を扱った——本稿はその関手が対を持つ場合を見る。論文179 は「構成できない」に別根があると示した——第6節は存在するのに一意でないという第四の場合である。 設定。二つの操作が随伴であるとは、おおよそ、片方で作った対象からの写像と、元の対象からもう片方で落とした先への写像とが一対一に対応することを言う。「余計なものを足す」操作と「捨てる」操作が対になっているという形である。本稿は、対になっていない構成を名指す。 第一に、対になっていることは数で確かめられる。n 個の生成元を持つ自由群から群への準同型の個数は、随伴が正しければ相手の元を n 個自由に選ぶことと同じであり、位数の n 乗ちょうどでなければならない。位数 6 の巡回群と三次対称群では、n が 1、2、3 のとき 6、36、216 になる。位数 8 の二面体群と四元数群では 8、64、512 になる。個数が群の構造に一切依らない——可換かどうかが違うのに、どちらも 216 である。自由群から見ると、相手の中身が見えない。見えているのは元の個数だけである。 第二に、自由でない相手からは冪にならない。巡回群からの準同型、すなわち n 乗して単位元になる元を数えると、n が 2 のとき二面体群で 6、四元数群で 2 になる。位数 8 の冪ではない。そして今度は相手の中身が見えている——同じ位数の二つの群が、違う数を返した。分離子はここにある。巡回群は自由ではなく、関係式を課している。関係式を課した分だけ、相手の構造が答に効いてくる。「自由」とは、関係式が一つも無いことである。 第三に、これが本稿の芯である。空間を閉じた空間に埋め込む操作をコンパクト化といい、二つある。一点コンパクト化は無限遠に点を一つ足し、実数直線を円にする。ストーン=チェックのコンパクト化は可能な限り大きく足す。開区間から実数直線へのただの包含写像を取り、一点コンパクト化に延長できるかを調べると、できない。開区間の無限遠点は両端の両方から近づかれるのに、包含写像はその二つを実数直線の内点へ送り、実数直線の無限遠点はそこにない。一点に送りたいのに、行き先が二つある。したがって一点コンパクト化は、連続写像の圏の上で関手ですらない。関手になるのは固有写像に制限したときだけである。随伴かどうか以前に、対応が写像を運ばない。一方ストーン=チェックは左随伴である。 第四に、完備化は写像の種類を決めるまで随伴でない。距離空間の完備化は、一様連続写像を許せば随伴になり、リプシッツ写像でも随伴になり、連続写像だけを許すと随伴でなくなる。理由は簡単で、連続写像はコーシー列をコーシー列に送らないので、完備化へ延ばす先が決まらない。一様連続性は、まさにそれを保証するために置かれている。「完備化は自由構成である」と書くとき、どの圏の話かを書かなければならない。 第五に、代数的閉包は随伴ではない。体には代数的閉包が存在し、「余計なものを足して閉じる」という完備化とよく似た形をしている。ところが普遍性が成り立たず、代数閉体への写像が一意に決まらない。有理数体の代数的閉包には、恒等写像でない自己同型が無数にある。存在するのに、一意でない。論文179 は「構成できない」に三つの別根があると示したが、これは第四の場合である——構成できるが、標準的な構成が無い。随伴でないことは欠陥ではなく、代数的閉包は完全に有用な構成である。言うのは、「自由構成」という一語で括るとこの違いが消えるということだけである。 結び。「余計なものを足す」構成は、三段に分かれた。写像を運ばないもの、運ぶが対を持たないもの、対を持つもの。分離子も三段である。そもそも写像を運ぶか。運ぶとして、対を持つか。対を持つとして、どの圏でか。「自由構成」「完備化」「閉包」といった語は、どれも同じ形に見えて、対の有無が違う。対を持つかどうかは、Hom の個数を数えれば見える——位数の冪になるかどうか、それだけである。 作成にあたって:本稿の着想と内容は、著者自身の考察に基づくものです。文章の構成整理や英訳、数式の確認には AI(大規模言語モデル)の助力を得ました。最終的な内容の解釈や誤りがあれば、それらはすべて著者の責に帰します。お気づきの点があれば、ご教示いただければ幸いです。
