title: National Socialism and the End of Modernity
abstract: Nazism provides an interesting test case with which to evaluate modernity's utility as concept and historical lens. More than most other recent historical phenomena and issues, the Third Reich has provoked intense scrutiny of its relationship to the modern world.1 Since the 1930s, analysts have wondered whether Nazism represented a throwback to a barbaric past or rather exemplified the worst of modernity, reflections that have continued up to the present, including a series of debates conducted since the 1980s in the wake of the loss of faith in modernization theory.2 A well-established narrative, in vogue in the 1960s and 1970s, of Nazism as the product of uneven development and of its exponents as searchers for a mythical past gave way to a recognition that in its roots and impulses Nazism drew on and expressed recognizable and widespread modern developments. Ever since then, the disturbing evidence of the Nazis' contemporaneity has both reflected and influenced our thinking about modernity.3 Yet while the Nazis cannot be explained away by reference to some kind of special departure from the modern world, the concept of modernity has proven surprisingly unhelpful as diagnosis and explanation. The problem is partly our lack of clarity about what modernity means, partly that in rejecting older modernization theories' normative assumptions we have often produced a new moralizing counter-narrative about modernity's “fatal potential,” and partly that the Nazis were a product far more of their particular epoch than of a generic modern.4 This, in turn, is an indicator less of Nazi specialness per se than of the fact that the basic ingredients of modernity allow for such massively varying societal outcomes and such huge differences between successive epochs as to give modernity very little explanatory power. For the modernization theories of the 1950s, Nazism was something of a provocation, since it was industrially modern but neither pluralistic nor benign.5 Whereas Stalinism and to a certain extent Italian fascism could be explained as developmental dictatorships, Nazism—despite the efforts of some authors—did not easily fit into this pattern.6 Instead, it proved easier to read as development gone wrong, a sign that the interlocking mechanisms that made up the modernization syndrome could get horribly out of sync. In the model of the German special path, or Sonderweg, feudal elites were seen as having manipulated the political system, substituting chauvinistic and radical ideologies for genuine representation, and allowing an irrational and anti-modern movement to emerge and eventually gain political power.7 Much of this theorizing related to German society before 1933; Nazi Germany was the vanishing point for accounts of Germany's special path rather than the principal site at which the application of modernization theory took place.8 However, some authors used modernization theory to attribute the regime's dysfunctional character to its lack of pluralism and rational structures.9 Because it was clear that the regime had nevertheless made substantial use of modern technology, it was seen as exemplifying a kind of reactionary modernism.10 As modernization theory in general became discredited, so the Sonderweg approach in German history came under attack—particularly in its view of the limits to bourgeois influence and its emphasis on the power and influence of feudal groups.11 The spread of new kinds of right-wing politics in Wilhelmine Germany, for example, was now no longer attributed to continuing feudal influence, but rather was seen as a bourgeois response to the challenge to its leadership posed by the emergence of mass politics at a time of rapid change.12 This, in turn, encouraged new ways of thinking about Nazism's roots and goals. Since the appearance of Detlev Peukert's book Volksgenossen und Gemeinschaftsfremde in 1982, most references to modernity in work on Nazism have underlined the ways in which Nazism exemplified features of modernity or was born of a thoroughly modern crisis.13 From being an aberration from modernization, Nazism had become the quintessential manifestation of modernity. Once the lens of classical modernization theory was cast aside, it became clear that Nazi electoral support did not come from marginal, backwards-oriented groups and that the Nazis were not promising or seeking to escape from the framework of an industrial society.14 To be sure, the Nazis, like their fascist counterparts in Italy, prized the racial value of yeoman rural stock, but this was a common trope of contemporary racial theory, and certainly no effort to turn back the clock.15 Hitler himself was impatient with attacks on big business for the sake of the small man.16 Industrial strength, affluent consumers, rural racial virtues, a vast tame agricultural hinterland—all of these belonged to his notion of the Germany of the future.17 Moreover, it also became clear that the early post-1945 decades had seen the suppression of many aspects of other contemporary societies that would have suggested that Nazism was in tune with contemporary trends.18 Nowhere was this more evident than in the way that knowledge of the global support for Social Darwinism and eugenics was suppressed in the wake of revelations about Nazism.19 In the era of classical modernization theory, Nazism thus looked more like an aberration than it should have. Finally, though this remains more contentious, it was far from clear that Nazism had proven so dysfunctional, in the sense either that popular discontent had forced it into war or that the regime's trajectory was the product of uncontrolled radicalization. If neither the Nazis nor many of their supporters were looking backward (except in the sense that all nationalists call on past myths and symbols), what did it mean to say that they were modern? Did it mean that the regime largely resembled its contemporaries, and the Third Reich was following or mirroring trends of neighboring societies? Was the point rather that its profile was distinctive but nonetheless made of modern clay? Or was it recognizably modern only in its point of departure—a thoroughly modern crisis—but with a subsequent trajectory that was sui generis? The striking variation in answers to these questions is not surprising on one level, given the hideous juxtapositions the Nazi regime has to offer, but on another it reveals the very considerable uncertainties as to what exactly modernity is and what it looks like. We can see this uncertainty in the terminology itself. Although “modernity” and “the modern” have emerged as the most influential concepts, “modernization”—admittedly different in its implications from older theories—has nevertheless retained an important place.20 A small number of influential pieces have tried “modernism” on for size as a substitute for both terms.21 Should modernity be understood as a set of common processes, albeit ones without the benign political associations they used to have? If so, the concept of modernization continues to be useful. If modernity is better conceptualized as a set of potentials or propensities, then “modernity” itself may be the preferred term.22 Or should we be thinking rather of a state of mind or a claim made at various points in history—the kind of claim that, as Frederick Cooper put it, justified colonization—or perhaps the kind of dream of the future that encouraged dazzling new city visions?23 If so, we may be moving into the territory of modernism.24 These different usages map onto different ways of conceptualizing Nazism's relationship to the modern world. For example, “modernization” tends to be deployed for arguments that Nazism responded to social problems or pursued policies that were similar to those of neighboring societies.25 Modernity and modernism, by contrast, tend to be preferred in work that foregrounds the distinctiveness of Nazi goals and actions but diagnoses some underlying potential in modern society to which Nazism gave disturbing expression.26 In short, the conceptual terrain reveals the plasticity in conceptualizations both of the modern world and of the Nazis' connection to it. A glance at recent work on the Nazis as modernizers also reveals how difficult it has proved to classify social change since the signposts offered by the classical theories of modernization were dismantled. The most sophisticated efforts have come from Michael Prinz and Rainer Zitelmann, who saw Nazism as responding to the same challenges of renewal and development facing other industrial societies at the time of the world economic crisis.27 Alongside their work, other authors claimed that the Nazis were offering innovative solutions to the economic crisis as “Keynesians before Keynes,” or noted among other things the moves by the German Labor Front to promote productivity and the rational use of labor or to remove the status barriers between blue- and white-collar workers in pursuit of a mobile and motivated workforce.28 In 1933, Germany clearly did not stop being part of a transatlantic conversation about rationalization and effective man-management. Even within the SS, the men of the Business Administration Main Office combined a strong belief in the regime's priorities with a commitment to efficiency and modern management.29 Yet given the obvious political differences between Nazism and other major industrial powers, it is clear that Nazi modernization cannot be subsumed under the classic notion of an interlocking syndrome, in which a given set of economic, social, and political developments necessarily fit together in a standard pattern. Some authors tried to address this with talk of “partial modernization,” but then there was no longer a coherent sense of which developments were necessary or how they were functionally interrelated.30 Classical theories had a clear measure of successful modernization, namely the development of pluralism and democracy, but the measure of modernity for newer work was much less obvious. It was reasonable for Prinz to claim that we should not write off the Nazis' deprofessionalization of welfare through the winter-help scheme as anti-modern, given the cyclical nature of governmental initiatives in the modern era more generally, or for other authors to identity the modern elements in Nazi agrarian and environmental policies.31 As long as the claim that the Nazis were willing modernizers is merely reactive, offering a critique of earlier modernization theory, it has traction: we can agree that, say, pro-agricultural policies are not necessarily a sign of romantic anti-modernism. But the challenge then is to identify—particularly in the short to medium term—what policy trend would definitively not count as modernization. Then again, no one was claiming the Holocaust as modernization or arguing that a Germany that had carried out the mass murder of part of its population had thereby been modernized. Unlike the older literature, the newer work thus had no ready-made way of explaining the Nazis' exceptionality. At times the foregrounding of consumer dreams and the forgetting of mass murder seemed almost distasteful.32 The most influential conclusions about Nazism and modernity thus have not come from studies that focused on modernization as a set of “secular” processes but can rather be found in work from the Frankfurt School, through Detlev Peukert to Zygmunt Bauman and Giorgio Agamben, identifying essential connections between Nazism's most striking and disturbing features and “modernity,” here understood as a set of potentials or inherent impulses.33 Influenced by Michel Foucault, historians have been increasingly aware of the repertoire of biopolitics that emerged in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and of eugenics' growing influence in the twentieth-century United States and Europe.34 Within Germany, eugenics had by the 1920s become a staple element in much social and medical policy discourse.35 This biopolitics involved not just state ambition, but the increasing role of scientific knowledge (or at least knowledge that claimed scientific status) and specialist elites in shaping policy and discourse.36 A second, related argument has linked the Nazis' embrace of selective racial engineering to the crisis of the welfare state. For Peukert, Germany was particularly vulnerable to calls for selective engineering because its advanced welfare state created ambitions and expectations that were not likely to survive economic crisis.37 While Nazi antisemitism cannot be subsumed under quite the same narrative of efficiency and selectivity, here too there have been important arguments about the function and logic of murder in the context of Nazi imperial expansion.38 At the broadest level, Bauman has argued that the Holocaust continued in relatively pure form—since territory and national competition were not at stake—a modern “garden culture,” in which the state seeks to weed out the unfit and create a pure society. title: Rapunzel and the Ivory Tower: How Open Access Will Save the Humanities (from Themselves)
abstract: There is no single open access debate. Instead, the open access debate refers to a variety of concerns from a fluctuating body of stakeholders. As there is little hope for sufficiently addressing them all in so brief a space, this article will limit itself to the debate surrounding the role of open access within the humanities within the UK, particularly within the discipline of history. It will argue that open access can facilitate the healing of disciplinary fractures and reconnect academic scholarship to the wider public debate. It will conclude with a brief examination of the current publishing ecosystem and how open access should affect stakeholders therein. The historical profession is growing, as is the number of interdisciplinary scholars for whom historical knowledge is a critical aspect of their research. Statistics provided by the American Historical Association and the Institute of Historical Research show significant increases in the number of history postgraduates, despite growing sentiment that employment opportunities are dwindling.1 In order to accommodate these postgraduate practitioners, historical research has become increasing specialized, increasingly fragmented into sub-fields or even smaller groupings.2 This is reflected by both increasing specificity within dissertation titles and in the absolute number of academic publishing venues, the latter suggesting a need for new discursive spaces for these sub-specialisms. No longer is the historical community sufficiently served by a small number of printed journals; no longer is there a conversation through which the profession or even a field can be kept fully abreast. Journal specialization has economic repercussions. The greater the number of specialist journals, the more difficult it is for an institution, or individual academic, to obtain regular access to the complete debate. There are several solutions to this problem, all with legitimate difficulties. The creation of electronic super-journals has the virtue of simplicity, but is thought to dismiss the importance of curation within particular niches and specialisms. Although the forthcoming Open Library of Humanities – advocated by Martin Eve in his conclusion – has already posited a number of niche curation possibilities within its super-journal framework, Paul Kirby notes that the existence of myriad independent journals allows an author's work ‘to be read in a certain tradition, and in the wake of particular historical arguments’ and that the desire to present work to a particular audience ‘is not unreasonable’.3 Although a super-repository would not necessarily prevent a work from reaching its intended audience, neither would the research necessarily come to the attention of a particular society's membership should they continue traditional, independent publication. More importantly, perhaps an absolute reliance upon like-minded audiences is an unreasonable aim. The dangers, if not the inevitability, of groupthink are well documented and by cloistering our work into ever smaller, sympathetic repositories, we risk falling into a self-perpetuating echo chamber.4 Thus, for the sake of the discipline, pressure towards centralization, though by no means inevitable, is perhaps one worthy of yielding to. Providing open access to academic scholarship is not the only solution to this fracturing of disciplinary discourse; indeed, increased funding for subscriptions to and indexing of academic research within the scholarly community might well achieve similar aims, should such funding become available. However, we must not forget that for all the virtues of the ivory tower, academic historians do not live within a closed ecosystem. Popular historians, as well as amateur enthusiasts, perform important roles in shapingour understanding of the past. Works by these authors are often more readily accessible to the public through relatively inexpensive books, television or cinematic presentations – such as the recent television production of Philippa Gregory's The White Queen – or through free web resources – such as Wikipedia and Spartacus Educational. The academic merit of these works is beyond the remit of this essay, but has been elaborated upon elsewhere.5 What is crucial here is their active involvement in the public debate. Public consensus on historical fact is, in many ways, being forged on the battlefields of Wikipedia and other online knowledge brokers. Academia's relative absence from this debate is noteworthy. For example, despite recent scholarly attention to W.T. Stead, including a centenary conference, his Wikipedia article contains just 33 footnotes, a third of which point to an open access repository of his writings.6 Of the rest, four refer to works in the public domain, three to scholarship distributed by academic publishers, five to commercial publishers and the remainder to online news articles. Moreover, the references to public domain works were extracted from a cited popular history that was itself made available on the cited online repository. Despite the appallingly cyclical nature of these references, this is not evidence of Wikipedia's scholarly failure. On the contrary, Wikipedia's guidelines necessitate accurate citation for all assertions and give prominence to those that are immediately verifiable by other users. Indeed, even a brief examination of the entry's talk page demonstrates the extent to which editors exercised scholarly rigour in its creation, with more than 450 edits over nine years.7 Thus, by failing to make recent academic research freely accessible, both academic and public understanding remains shockingly underdeveloped.8 The paucity of involvement by academics, through editing articles or by allowing publicly verifiable citation of their work, may be partially explained by the need for credit. The continuing pressure to publish or perish, in the form of traditional journals, has led to the belief that contributing to public forums will not result in career progression or raise academic profiles within a field; therefore, it is considered a waste of limited time.9 As for making their academic work easily accessible, the need for credit, and intellectual ownership, has led many to demonstrate outright fear of their work being used outside the limited context in which it was originally produced. Indeed, one of the most contentious aspects of the recent RCUK guidelines for open-access dissemination is the CC BY requirement, a debate raised by both James Emmott and Peter Mandler elsewhere in this forum. Emmott provides an admirable explanation of the nature and history of an author's moral rights to his or her own work, but the full implications of this are perhaps best understood next to a close examination of the copyright license itself. According to (3.7.i) of the RCUK policy document, any article distributed under the gold open access scheme must use the Creative Commons CC BY licence, which allows attributed use and ‘remixing’ for commercial and non-commercial derivatives.10 Although attributed use remains standard practice under UK and international fair use legislation, provisions for creating derivative works have led to significant apprehension within in the academic community. The Royal Historical Society, for instance, recently described the protection as allowing ‘others to use your work for their own commercial purposes, and which permits mixing of your work with the work of others without specifying which is which, i.e. what we tell our students is plagiarism’.11 This interpretation of the license, like the earlier editors' statement discussed by Emmott, reflects significant concerns that academic work distributed under CC BY will be open to misrepresentation, misuse and intellectual property theft by commercial and other organizations. However, the full legal documentation explicitly states in (4b) that any work that uses material from the article must provide the name of the original author, along with a URL or publication information for the original work, and to do so ‘in a manner at least as prominent as the credits for the other contributing authors’.12 They must also clearly indicate how the work has been adapted and ‘may not implicitly or explicitly assert or imply any connection with, sponsorship or endorsement by the Original Author’ without that author's express written permission. Section (4c) further protects the author by stating that the user cannot ‘distort, mutilate, modify or take other derogatory action in relation to the Work which would be prejudicial to the Original Author's honor or reputation’. Finally, a user must, upon request, remove attribution to the original author from any work the original author deems inferior to or a misrepresentative of the original material. Although infringements of these rights have rarely resulted in civil litigation, a fact that Creative Commons believes demonstrates the licenses' robust construction, some legal precedents have already been set in favour of the original creator.13 Finally, as the rights retained by the author under the written terms of the CC BY licence exceed those currently offered by many traditional publishing venues, and are intellectually congruent with academic fair use provisions, its classification as a facilitator of plagiarism or intellectual property theft is difficult to justify.14 Indeed, by making the original material freely available, and requiring robust attribution, those viewing remixed material are encouraged and empowered to examine the original work, greatly reducing the chance of misrepresentations and increasing the impact of, or credit given to, the original. Open access is not merely a way to reduce library subscription costs, but to make material available and relevant to a genuinely interested and engaged public audience.15 Should we squander this engagement, history's continued existence in academia may very well be in jeopardy. Yet, even if these ideological drives towards open access are accepted, we cannot ignore the practical effects it will have on stakeholders – individual authors, learned societies and publishers – all of whom are faced with crises of authority and relevance. Heretofore, the crisis of authorship has centred on the charging of Article Processing Charges (APCs) and how best to accommodate the shift from pay-to-read to pay-to-publish models. As the other contributors have addressed this, my discussion will instead focus on the crisis of authority. As the web has expanded, so too has the number of individuals able to publish their writing. This has led accusations of a ‘wild west’ of information, wherein fact and fabrication become interchangeable owing to their equal accessibility.16 It is likewise feared that, within academia, open access will reduce scholarly rigour, making access to well executed research meaningless as traditional indicators of authority, such as publication-space scarcity in high-reputation journals, are no longer relevant.17 Academics will lose their privileged positions as arbiters of knowledge, meticulously earned through years of study, and fact will fall prey to the tyranny of the mob. In light of research demonstrating the relative effectiveness of democratically assembled online knowledge, Ziyad Marar has noted that, in contrast to scholarly research, Wikipedia ‘does a different job and does it extremely well. But how does original, high quality information and knowledge get produced to start with?’18 Like opponents of open source software, opponents of (non-APC) open access argue that artificial scarcity, and a closed, carefully guarded process of accreditation, ensures the legitimate authority of authors. Like proponents of open source software, supporters of free-to-read-and-publish open access argue that ‘if everyone can see the code [or sourcework], and test it, flaws will be easier to find, and because the process of implementation is tested in public, everyone can trust the product’.19 Thus, good scholarship will rest not on the ‘private, unaccountable, final word’ of two unknown peer reviewers, but on an article's continued merit in light of constant review.20 Moreover, concerns about permanency, about maintaining a single, authoritative version others may cite, are easily resolved by including a version number within the citation; indeed, this is little different from citing editions of monographs. Learned societies, too, face a crisis of authority. Their roles as foci for debates, as providers of funding, training and certification, and as gatekeepers of academic quality are not controversial. Indeed, the crisis is not they will be cast aside, but that they will wither from a lack of funding should subscription revenue dissipate.21 Although revenue streams vary considerably, it is worth considering the idea that the removal of journal subscriptions need not necessitate the abandonment of membership fees.The intrinsic joy felt by some when handling a hard-copy publication duly acknowledged, the value of a society is not necessarily its provision of twenty-some articles a year, but in its creation of a scholarly community, manifested in meetings, workshops and research support. Moreover, with library subscriptions reduced, institutions may find funds available to sponsor individual memberships, something that rarely occurs in the current environment. Conversely, the role of the publisher, particularly the commercial publisher, in this ecosystem is one of particular debate; much sighing and eye rolling has accompanied claims of their utter irrelevancy and their paramount importance to the publication of high-quality scholarship. Their value is seemingly based upon the services that they offer to editors and authors. The precise nature of these is difficult to discern, as no systematic evaluation of their costs has been made available, but anecdotal evidence suggests their most important offerings are copy-editing and typesetting, distribution and marketing, and the bestowing of credibility and prestige.22 The most legitimate, or at least evidenced, of these is that commercial and not-for-profit publishers offer credibility and prestige to journals and authors. As the recently debuted Transgender Studies Quarterly noted, having the support of an established publishing firm lends much needed legitimacy to niche or emerging sub-fields.23 This same instinct encourages recent graduates to submit their dissertations only to the most prestigious university presses or the most competitive journals; although the quality of a manuscript should dictate its reception by the academic community, it would be unreasonable to ignore these very real, if illegitimate, pressures.Yet, as consumers of scholarly material, and especially when hiring new staff, should we not be prepared to forgo our reliance on short-cut indicators of quality and demonstrate at least a modicum of critical interest in the quality of the academic work before us? The second service, distribution, is wholly unnecessary in a digital ecosystem. The distribution of a digitally composed and typeset document by means of an online repository requires virtually no additional expenditure on the part of the author or editorial board beyond the existing maintenance of the web platform. Like all online material, it instantly becomes freely accessible to anyone with an unfiltered internet connection. Yet, some critics warn of the arrogance of this digital turn. Brienza argues that it is incorrectly assumed that open access material, simply by being digital, will be freely accessible throughout the world. She argues that ‘one needs an Internet connection and sufficient new media literacy to locate desired research adrift amid vast seas of online content. The number of people globally even the latter excludes is obviously very high.’24 What she neglects here is an acknowledgement of the rapid expansion of fixed and mobile broadband throughout the developing world, the commensurate growth of digital literacy, and the significantly higher barriers to obtaining, cataloguing and storing a hard-copy scholarly library in these communities.25 As for marketing, that publishers help create name-recognition for newer journals does not negate the reality that demonstrable quality, and ease of access, are increasingly becoming more effective than the distribution of flyers and catalogues to conferences and under-funded institutional libraries.26 The final and most commonly cited service is that of typesetting and copyediting. Although they are often unsatisfied with the quality of copyediting provision, much of which is outsourced to non-disciplinary providers, journal editors simply cannot provide these services directly, especially when working gratis. The plight of editors is easily sympathized with, but the solution should be equally apparent. If a work is not properly composed, does not conform to the stated style requirements, or requires significant grammatical attention, it should not be accepted for peer review, but returned to the author with a kindly notice that it should undergo an additional draft. We rail against students for their lack of care and attention to formal writing standards and yet we expect that a publisher will transform our mediocre writing in order to present our arguments in the best possible light; this is nonsense. As for non-native speakers, or those with genuine difficulties in written communication, would university resources not be better spent on improving the writing of its academics – or indeed providing institutional copy-editing – than on outsourcing this service via article-processing charges? For those outside institutions, their plight is no different from the thousands of freelance authors who submit articles for magazine and newspaper publication. To establish authority as an academic scholar, you must be able to convey your thoughts in an intelligible manner without excessive interference from either overworked editors or unaccountable commercial firms; an uncomfortable reality, perhaps, but one with which we must come to terms. In the end, this short discussion has advocated a fundamental reintegration of scholarship within and beyond academic publishing. For those who fear the wild west of the world wide web, I direct your attention to a brief plea, written 15 years ago, by essayist Christopher Hitchens.
