title: “Man is the Story-Telling Animal”: Graham Swift’sWaterland, Ecocriticism and Narratology
abstract: But man—let me offer you a definition—is the story-telling animal. Wherever he goes he wants to leave behind not a chaotic wake, not an empty space, but the comforting marker-buoys and trail-signs of stories. He has to go on telling stories, he has to keep on making them up. As long as there’s a story, it’s all right. Graham Swift’s 1983 novel Waterland was one of the first British novels that ecocritics read as an example of postmodern fiction that can also yield a productive ecocritical reading.1 The novel can also be analyzed from another critical intersection that as yet has been unexplored: that of ecocriticism and narratology. A narratology-inflected ecocriticism foregrounds the shaping role that narratives and narrativity play in shaping our perceptions of the nonhuman natural world. With its emphasis on the natural landscape on the one hand and storytelling on the other, Waterland especially invites such an approach. Waterland is narrated by Tom Crick, a middle-aged London history teacher. Faced with early retirement, he departs from the set curriculum and, instead of teaching his pupils about the French Revolution, tells them his own history and that of the region he grew up in, the Fens in eastern England. While his professional and personal life crumbles—Crick’s wife is admitted to a mental hospital after kidnapping a baby from a supermarket—he recalls the events of his youth. These are alternated with stories of his beer-brewing forefathers, the Atkinsons, and tales of natural history about the landscape of the Fens and its nonhuman inhabitants such as the eel. In one of the most extensive ecocritical analyses of the novel, Karla Armbruster provides an overview of mainly non-ecocritical responses to the work, and advocates treating “the land/waterscape [in Waterland] in its own right” (20), rather than approaching the Fenland setting as merely metaphor. She cites Michael Gorra’s interpretation of the novel as an example of such a metaphorical approach: “The Fens are the physical embodiment of a history in which all progress is chimerical” (Gorra 393). Likewise emphasizing the metaphorical dimension of the landscape, Evelyn Cobley remarks that “the Fens function both literally as geographical location and figuratively as metaphor for the ways in which the narrator and his characters seek to make sense of what they experience” (277). Ecocriticism, Armbruster argues, is taken out of its “comfort zone” (24) by Waterland which demonstrates that the cultural constructedness of the concept of nature does not necessarily deny the existence of a physical reality outside of a text (21). Postmodern concepts, she proposes, can “challenge ecocriticism to question some of its basic assumptions, including the idea that the solutions to our environmental problems can be based on unchanging truths or standards found in nature as well as the notion that literature can give us simple access to such truths” (23). Other scholars as well have explored Waterland primarily as an illustration for the ways in which ecocriticism and postmodernism meet and intersect.2 Serpil Oppermann, for instance, presents a reading of the novel from the perspective of what she terms postmodern ecocriticism. The “postmodern ecocritical theory” (119) she applies to the novel has three main features: it questions hierarchical, dualistic systems (118), examines the presence or absence of constructions of nature in the discourses that literary works employ (121–22), and draws attention to the linguistic strategies underlying definitions of nature (117). The ecocritical study of much contemporary fiction is indeed, as Oppermann suggests, long overdue,3 and a particular subset of contemporary literature that she calls “ecological postmodern fictions” proves to be particularly valuable for ecocritical analysis. While the term “ecological postmodern fictions” may be unfortunate in limiting analysis to a relatively small portion of contemporary literature, Oppermann’s suggestion that these fictions “raise the issues of how reality is discursively constructed and sustained, how discourse shapes our world, and how it governs the way we think about reality” (248) holds true for these works as well as those that are not ecological postmodern fictions. Indeed, the discursivity that Oppermann emphasizes is, as I shall discuss in more detail below, a key part of all texts, and its analysis should therefore not be limited to postmodern literature alone. Yet critics such as Armbruster and Oppermann have so far not critically examined the part played by storytelling in the depiction of the nonhuman natural environment. The full significance of the natural world in Waterland, however, is not revealed until attention it paid to not only what is described, but also how literary and narratological form shape representations of the Fenlands. In what follows I explore this dimension by discussing how the combination of the framework narrative and the fairy tale genre provide an environmental layer to the novel. This layer emphasizes the instability of the landscape, the role of stories in achieving a sense of environmental care, and a trans-corporeal awareness of human–nature relations. To provide a setting for this reading I will first discuss at more length the importance of narratives to Waterland in general, particularly that of stories about the nonhuman natural world. The significance of the Fens to Waterland is illustrated early on in the novel by a lengthy chapter on the region, which provides a setting for Crick’s narratives that is both “palpable and unreal” (8). These stories are the primary strategy by which the Fens are constructed as more than mere background or metaphor in the novel, but as a unique place: a space that is physically distinct and humanly meaningful. The way in which this is achieved echoes ecocritical and bioregional thought in which narratives of place—whether about people or nature, public or private histories—are seen as means of passing on information of a region, as well as expressing and contributing to place-attachment.4 The Fens, Crick tells his pupils, are a “fairy-tale land” (18) which for centuries has invited stories. The Cricks’ knack for storytelling sets them apart from the financially more successful Atkinsons, Tom Crick’s maternal ancestors: “While the Atkinsons made history, the Cricks spun yarns” (17). Crick’s father, for example, tells stories to explain natural phenomena to his sons, such as the stubborn flatness of the Fens themselves: “Why are the Fens flat? To which my father replied, first letting his face take on a wondering and vexed expression and letting his lips form for a moment the shape of an ‘O’: ‘Why are the Fens flat? So God has a clear view … ’” (13–14). Narratives are also the means by which the Cricks come to terms with the world around them and the experiences of their own lives. For instance, the stories that Crick tells his London students help him make sense of his own past—and troubled present. Moreover, stories told and heard in Waterland may also be interpreted as means of escaping reality: as Ronald McKinney puts it, “either we are bored with the dullness of reality or we are overwhelmed at its savage capacity to upset all our fictive quests for order, in which case, we invent new ‘histories’ to recover our serenity” (826).5 Similarly, George Landow proposes that stories are the Fenlanders’ way of assuaging their fear (201).6 However, while Landow suggests that Waterland is consequently “suspicious of all story-telling” (203), I would argue that both Crick and the novel as a whole employ and emphasize stories to demonstrate the interplay of narratological form and content in the textual formation of landscape. To put it differently, Waterland is not so much suspicious of storytelling as that it acknowledges the inescapability of narrativization in representing and making sense of the world. Rather than fighting this, the novel embraces storytelling by combining a wide variety of stories and genres. Crick specifically uses stories as part of a larger strategy of including and excluding often employed in place-making: that which is believed to belong to a certain area is included and emphasized, and as such replaces the stories, histories and values of that which is excluded. This technique is not only employed to reinforce the power of the center—recall the phrase “if you’re not with us, you’re against us”—but can also be employed to advocate the region and regional identity, as Crick does. His lessons consequently illustrate the postmodern preference for small narratives rather than grand narratives, for pluriformity rather than homogeneity, for multiple truths rather than one truth. In Waterland this typically postmodern technique is used to create and strengthen the kind of place attachment and general attention to the natural environment that environmentalists have argued leads to environmental conservation. title: To Believe in Humanity and in Rehabilitation: Howard A. Rusk, MD, and the Birth of Rehabilitation Medicine
abstract: The last sentence in A World to Care For, the autobiography of Howard A. Rusk, MD, reads as follows: “To believe in rehabilitation is to believe in humanity” [1]. This very simple statement reflects a deeper meaning. The 2 interconnected beliefs expressed by Rusk are a belief in the importance of the patient's “ability to rehabilitate himself” and a confidence that “this third branch of medical responsibility will one day be accepted and practiced as readily throughout the world as the first two branches, prevention and definitive care, are now practiced” [1]. Rusk went on to say, “The sooner the people of the world demand rehabilitation services, the sooner they will get the services” [1]. These 2 beliefs are foundational to his life's work and the practice of physical medicine and rehabilitation (PM&R) today. They reflect Rusk's global perspective and advocacy for both patients with disabling medical conditions and the medical specialty of PM&R. As recounted in chapter 3 of his autobiography [2], Howard Archibald Rusk, MD, was born in 1901 in Brookfield, Missouri, a small midwestern town of 5000 inhabitants where he grew up. Rusk apprenticed with a local physician, Thomas P. Fore, MD. Starting in his early teens, Rusk ran errands and cleaned instruments in exchange for assisting with minor surgical procedures, medical emergencies, and other aspects of patient care. At the age of 17 years, Rusk left for college at the University of Missouri in Columbia, Missouri, during what turned out to be boom years for his father's business, both in furniture sales and undertaking. However, the economic crisis of 1920-1921, a harbinger of what was to follow in 1929, nearly prevented Rusk from returning for his junior year. To cover tuition and expenses, he washed laboratory glassware and worked as an orderly at the county's public hospital. A search for a summer job near his girlfriend, Gladys Houx, who lived in Marshall, Missouri, led to a position at the Missouri State “Colony for the Feeble-Minded and Epileptic,” a name that reflected the attitudes of that period in our history. Here Rusk witnessed injections of the barbiturate anticonvulsant phenobarbital, a newly developed treatment that, for the first time, gave physicians the means to control seizures in children and young adults. But he most certainly began to experience what life must have been like for people with disabilities. The state of medical education in the 1920s was still such that the University of Missouri offered only a 2-year medical degree, even after the release of the Flexner Report in 1910 [2a]. Rusk had entered this program in his third year of college and thus was completing it as a college senior. In recognizing the importance of a 4-year medical degree, Rusk transferred to the University of Pennsylvania in 1922. As it happened, the university's medical school had been among the first in the United States to teach the principles of exercise and physical modalities as part of its curriculum. In 1906, Robert Tait McKenzie, MD, was lecturing to medical students on the role of exercise in treating postural problems, pronation of the foot, spinal disorders, and other conditions. Lecture material was supplemented by demonstrations in electrotherapy, hydrotherapy, and thermotherapy by another physician, Joseph B. Nylin, MD. By the time Rusk arrived at the University of Pennsylvania, McKenzie had achieved international recognition for providing services to British military forces during World War I and, in 1918, for publishing Reclaiming the Maimed, a publication that described physical and rehabilitation interventions for war injuries, and a companion to his earlier textbook, Exercise in Education and Medicine [3-3b]. After graduating from the University of Pennsylvania, Rusk returned to St Louis for an internship at St Luke's Hospital in St Louis, and, he and Gladys were married. He began practicing internal medicine but soon gravitated toward academic activities at Washington University. In addition to teaching and helping oversee the internship program at St Luke's, he published clinical studies on urticaria in the Journal of the American Medical Association and, for example, other studies on the effect of a low carbohydrate diet on obesity [4]. Compensation for academic work was limited, and patient collections dropped precipitously during the Great Depression. Rusk described relying on examinations for insurance companies as the mainstay of his income during that period. This created yet another opportunity for him to hone his musculoskeletal and neurologic examination skills and to develop skills in functional assessment. It is not clear what direction Rusk's career would have taken had the United States not entered World War II. Unlike other early pioneers in the field of PM&R, Rusk's medical career had not begun with a focus on either physical or rehabilitation medicine. For 15 years, he was a successful and busy physician practicing internal medicine in St Louis. Indeed, he was the second physician in the United States to become certified in internal medicine, a newly created specialty in 1930 [5]. Rusk responded to the onset of World War II by immediately joining the Air Force, which was still a division of the Army at that time, as a major (Figure 1). Howard Rusk, MD, Colonel in the Army Air Force early in his World War II career. (Photo courtesy of Howard Rusk Jr.) Air Force hospitals alone cared for 50,000 soldiers a day by that point. The pressing need for military manpower meant that medical care in those hospitals was geared toward return to active duty whenever possible, and Rusk gained an early appreciation for this task at his first military post, Jefferson Barracks outside of St Louis. Rusk brought his success at returning soldiers to active duty to the attention of the chief of the Air Force's medical branch, Brigadier General David N. W. Grant. Rusk was subsequently commissioned to introduce his multidimensional rehabilitation program in all 253 Air Force hospitals. Over time, as Rusk gained more experience as a physician, his concept of rehabilitation grew and broadened, such that he realized that it was not enough just to treat a person's medical condition without understanding the patient in the context of his life and work. He stated, “we had to worry about his emotional, social, education, and occupational needs as well. We had to treat the whole man and we had to teach his friends and family how to accept him and help him in his new condition” [6].. During World War II, Rusk began his long relationship with Bernard Baruch, the wealthy adviser to U.S. presidents and the son of Simon Baruch, MD, who was a national expert in hydrology and hydrotherapy in the early 20th century (Figure 2). Rusk suggested that other branches of the armed services should have a diverse rehabilitation program much as had been developed in the Air Force. Bernard Baruch used his influence with President Franklin D. Roosevelt, who, in turn, instructed the secretary of war, Henry L. Stimson, to develop similar programs, including not only medical care and medical rehabilitation but also resocialization and psychosocial adjustment [7]. Howard Rusk with financier Bernard Baruch. (Photo courtesy of The State Historical Society of Missouri.) President Franklin Roosevelt died on April 12, 1945, and was succeeded by Harry Truman. Germany surrendered in May 1945, and Truman asked Rusk, a fellow Missourian and long-time friend, to join the group that was traveling to Potsdam to discuss plans for the end of the war and plans for peace in Europe. His role was as personal physician to Commanding General Hap Arnold, but Truman also wanted Rusk to meet with fellow Missourian General Omar Bradley, who had been appointed to reorganize the Veterans Administration (VA) [7]. General Bradley, a friend of Bernard Baruch, was familiar with the rehabilitation programs that Rusk had developed and wanted to see them be incorporated in the VA hospitals [8]. After the war, Rusk and Frank Krusen, MD, another early leader, were asked to be consultants in the development of the VA rehabilitation program, including the nation's first major inpatient rehabilitation service. By collaborating with Paul Magnuson, MD, who succeeded Major General Paul Hawley as medical director of the VA Health System, Rusk and Krusen helped establish rehabilitation services in all VA hospitals. More importantly, there was an emphasis in affiliation of VA hospitals with teaching hospitals and medical schools facilitating teaching [8]. Historian Richard Verville states, “By 1949, ten VA hospitals and four military hospitals had Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation residency training or fellowship programs, representing one third of the programs in the country” [9]. At the end of the war, Rusk dreamed of establishing the first comprehensive rehabilitation institute with a major academic affiliation in the United States. He saw that advancing the field of rehabilitation medicine would require a presence in the academic world, with greater interaction with other specialties, and he believed that this could best be accomplished in a large metropolitan area. Unfortunately, he was met with indifference in Missouri. In fact, one colleague referred to his rehabilitation ideas as “Rusk's Folly” [10]. After that humiliation, he moved to New York City with his wife and 3 children in December of 1945, taking significant personal and financial risks by leaving a thriving internal medicine practice in St Louis. Rusk was fortunate to be able to pursue his dream of an academic rehabilitation institute with the considerable support of many friends and colleagues who shared his vision, including George Deaver, MD, the medical director of the Institute for the Crippled and Disabled, and with significant support from Arthur Hayes Sulzberger, The New York Times publisher, who had been inspired by visiting the army rehabilitation centers that Rusk had helped develop during the war. With these allies, Rusk pitched his ideas to several medical schools in New York, and, with financial backing from Bernard Baruch, he was able to convince New York University (NYU) that the creation of a department of rehabilitation medicine was a worthwhile goal. He started as the inaugural chairman of the newly founded department in December 1946 and took a significant decrease in salary. However, he made another strategic move by accepting the position of medical editor at The New York Times, which gave him a bully pulpit to promote both his new department and the entire field of PM&R in those early years. He steadfastly wrote a weekly Times column for 23 years [11]. To further advance the field, Rusk spoke to “any crowd that would stand still at breakfast, lunch, tea, cocktails, dinner, or later in the evening” [12]. He provided, case by case, the evidence that rehabilitation interventions made disabled veterans independent, and, on average, increased wages for them from $148 to $1768 a year in 1945, a living wage in today's times. When speaking at public gatherings and through his weekly Times column, he emphasized how the airmen who were provided rehabilitation interventions were able to maintain their independence. During this period, Rusk was very active in treating patients in his new position at NYU, and he began to report remarkable results of rehabilitation interventions in civilian populations as well. Indeed, rehabilitation interventions could be effective in returning many civilians to independent living, just as had been demonstrated in the armed forces. In fact, the patients themselves became fierce advocates for rehabilitation medicine and rehabilitation services, and contributed to building community support. The groundswell of support from many sectors eventually resulted in the creation of the Institute for Rehabilitation Medicine (IRM) at NYU. Rusk's key collaborators in the initial development of the IRM included the New York Commissioner of Hospitals, Edward Bernecker, MD, and the mayor of New York City, William O'Dwyer, who accepted the proposal that the city's municipal hospitals would have a rehabilitation service. Subsequently, Rusk secured 2 floors of Bellevue Hospital and a few thousand dollars budget to set up the clinical service. This physical space, along with a pilot grant from Bernard Baruch, and the support of William Jacobs, MD, the administrator of Bellevue, made possible the opening of IRM [13]. The NYU-IRM program has since trained more than 1000 U.S. and international residents and 6000 medical students, and 19 of its alumni have become academic department chairs (New York University/IRM Residency Program, personal communication). With its success, the Bellevue rehabilitation service soon expanded to a donated building on East 38th Street and began to provide service to injured United Mine Workers and other patient populations. By 1952, programs had been established at various hospitals, including Bellevue, Goldwater Hospital, East 38th Street, City Hospital, Kings County, and Metropolitan. In addition, 35 young physicians were then in training [14]. Despite his claim of a dislike for fund-raising, Rusk was prodigiously successful at the task, convincing even skeptics of the importance of his mission. He raised additional funds from many New York philanthropists, and he was able to break ground for the new IRM in 1950, at an astronomical cost of 2 million dollars. All but $131,000 had been raised by the opening date. The IRM opened on January 25, 1951, as the first unit of the new NYU Medical Center. The new clinical environment allowed for even greater provision of care, and, with the successful treatment of prominent patients such as baseball legend Roy Campanella (who became quadriplegic at age 37 years as a result of a motor vehicle accident), the institution was firmly established as a center of clinical excellence (Figure 3). The IRM flourished under Rusk's leadership and ultimately received funding for rehabilitation medicine research as well [15]. Roy Campanella, Negro League and Major League (Brooklyn Dodgers) baseball player (seated) with Bernard Baruch, Howard Rusk, James Rosati (of Horizon House, a home for people with disabilities built on the grounds of NYU in the late 1950s). (Photo courtesy of The State Historical Society of Missouri.) A review of the early years of the NYU program would be lacking without the mention of the pioneer rehabilitation physician, George Deaver, MD. Upon his arrival in New York, Rusk formed a bond with Deaver and enlisted him as a colleague in developing the rehabilitation medicine department at NYU. George Deaver was most likely the first physician to establish a full-time practice in comprehensive rehabilitation medicine in the United States that included patients with spinal cord injury. He also developed the concept of activities of daily living, and he and his therapy staff developed an assessment system and checklist of 45 activities of daily living, a number that expanded over time [16]. title: Ask a Political Scientist: A Conversation with Michael S. Lewis-Beck about Vote Choice, Election Forecasting, and the 2022 Midterms
abstract: Previous articleNext article FreeAsk a Political Scientist: A Conversation with Michael S. Lewis-Beck about Vote Choice, Election Forecasting, and the 2022 MidtermsInterviewer: Mary Stegmaier and Interviewer: Charles TienInterviewer: Mary Stegmaier and Interviewer: Charles TienPDFPDF PLUSFull Text Add to favoritesDownload CitationTrack CitationsPermissionsReprints Share onFacebookTwitterLinked InRedditEmailQR Code SectionsMoreMary Stegmaier & Charles Tien:You have written extensively about voters, elections, and the economy in countries far and wide. We want to first ask you about the American voter. How have American voters changed or stayed the same over the last fifty years?Michael Lewis-Beck:When we co-authored The American Voter Revisited,1 an overriding question was whether the explanation of American electoral behavior, as articulated in The American Voter2 remained the same. We concluded that it did, as encapsulated in the classic funnel of causality, sorting determinants into long-term forces at the opening of the funnel, i.e., socio-demographics and party identification, and short-term forces at the tip of the funnel, i.e., issues and candidates. That explanation still fundamentally holds, in my view.The funnel can be sketched as a causal model, tracing out the direct and indirect paths to the vote choice. The diagram can be written as a set of equations to be estimated. Each equation contains conceptually the same variables over time. The slope coefficients of these variables can change, becoming stronger or weaker. The strength of the party identification coefficient has considerable interest, as it forms an indicator of the stability of the electoral system. However, the weights of the slope coefficients in the model are more inertial than commonly supposed, e.g., despite the presence of candidate Trump in 2016, Republican identifiers were no more likely to defect than Democratic identifiers from Clinton. Some of the weights do change, though. For example, social class seems to have less importance, as Democrats abandon their working-class base. Also, measurement of socio-demographics can change, even if the concept does not seem to. For example, take gender, where there is a move away from the simple dichotomous notion of male or female. Further, with regard to race and ethnicity, we see the increasing presence of Latinx voters is changing the measurement of that variable.MS & CT:The media environment has changed dramatically over the last fifty years. Has this impacted vote choice?MLB:The forms of media have changed greatly. For example, in surveys, media questions used to focus on newspapers, radio, TV, magazines. Now the whole internet apparatus has introduced various types of social media, e.g., Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, blogs. All this suggests big shifts in the sources of political information. Have these different sources of information made voters more knowledgeable about politics? The knee jerk reaction may be "yes." However, considerable survey research argues that voters are no more knowledgeable about US political institutions and electoral processes than they were fifty years ago. Furthermore, content analysis of the American National Election Study (ANES) open-ended questions, which allows voters to extensively express themselves about the political world, shows a limited amount of sophisticated content in how they connect the political dots, e.g., most don't really know much about what constitutes a "liberal" or a "conservative." The political framework of typical voters has loose logic and little connective tissue; in some ways their political brain works like a popcorn popper, e.g., random reactive kernels. To take an example, if one examines the open-ended responses of the 2016 ANES regarding negative opinions about Clinton, few mentions of ideology, issues, or demographics appear; often they just say, "I don't like her."MS & CT:Recent elections have taken place during a pandemic—the first pandemic in the modern era of public opinion polling. How has the pandemic impacted elections and voters? Will it have lasting effects?MLB:The electoral impact of COVID-19 has been pervasive, mostly hurting incumbents, who are blamed for the massive death and destruction. The Trump defeat in 2020 has been attributed to COVID, and more than one study has shown that his handling of that crisis cost him votes. However, at the same time, other key variables continued to operate per usual, e.g., Trump was also blamed for a faltering economy. Indeed, the impressive survey investigation by Clarke et al., shows that the two most important issues in the contest were COVID-19 and the economy.3 This is suggestive of the pandemic's role in the "causal funnel." COVID has emerged as an important issue, to be considered at the tip of the funnel. However, it has not driven out all other issues. Moreover, when it ceases to be an issue—and it will cease—its coefficient will become, effectively, zero.MS & CT:As you look toward the future, what do you think scholars of voting behavior and elections should focus on?MLB:In democracies, vote choice follows laws of electoral behavior. Since these laws are probabilistic, there may appear some fluctuation over time in the estimated weight, say, of the party identification variable. Nevertheless, the underlying process endures, e.g., Republican identifiers vote overwhelmingly for the Republican candidate, Democratic identifiers vote overwhelmingly for the Democratic candidate. The strength of this bond has survived serious challenge, e.g., in the 2016 presidential election, despite the apparent disparity of the candidates, party identification was an equivalent magnet for Democrats (87% for Clinton) and for Republicans (86% for Trump), according to our analysis of the ANES data.4 These fundamental processes deserve ongoing study, with the expectation that they are operating. More and more, the "journalistic fallacy" has become the dominant hypothesis. That is, observers assume the election at hand exists apart from past elections, with a de novo electorate moving into unchartered territory. That perspective may sell newspapers, but it tends to be false.MS & CT:How concerned are you that American elections will be less free and fair in 2022 and 2024?MLB:Voting means choosing your leaders. If potential leaders are not in competition, then choice doesn't exist. That's why organizations like Freedom House count "free and fair elections" as a critical component of a democratic system. Voters in democracies around the world count on free and fair elections as a presence and as a continued aspiration.When we say an election is "free and fair," that says there is no corruption or coercion, an ideal not always realized in the tumble of practical politics. Take the example credited, perhaps unjustly, to pols in Gary, Indiana, where the charge was to "vote early and vote often." In the United States, vote-buying or ballot box stuffing is not unheard of and sometimes there are unintentional errors, e.g., lost ballots or double counting. However, these deviations today are rare and, most importantly, they are scattered and local, e.g., in a precinct or town. At the margin, say a very tight mayoral race, the declared winner might actually have won with the help of faulty ballots. But these misfires are isolated, virtually never of a magnitude large enough to shift a national election. This healthy condition comes from the selection and integrity of the state officials chosen to set the rules. It's driven by trust on the ground level, in American communities, and I do not see that safety mechanism significantly changing; it's too planted in our soil. Cicero said something like, "whatever the character of the leader in the state, such was the character of the state." It's not the rules, it's the rule-makers that matter. Take the current example now, of partisan gerrymandering: while Republicans have had control over drawing more districts, the Democrats have still managed gains. That's the sort of give-and-take one could expect from a healthy democracy. Of course, threats are ever-present, e.g., courtroom challenges to the Voting Rights Act.MS & CT:These threats, do they worry you about the state of American democracy? What keeps you up at night?MLB:In the short-term, "yes," in the long-term, "no." Once a country firmly establishes a democratic form of government, it tends to have remarkable resiliency. Take the Latin American example, where democracy can be more fragile, in part simply because it has not been in place long enough.5 With respect to the US case, we have, for the first time in my memory, a large portion of the public who believe the 2020 presidential election was rife with ballot fraud, despite evidence to the contrary. That attitude, if persistent, will undermine the democratic functioning of our institutions. It will persist if the good people who are our leaders do nothing. As Jefferson said, "Give the people light, and they will show you the way." That means to me, as a political scientist, I should speak the truth as I know it. Our training, which has as its core the reasoned sifting of scientific evidence, gives us a special obligation in that regard. One piece of relevant empirical evidence seems especially encouraging: when liberal-conservative ideology is examined via the ANES surveys, the modal response remains "moderate"; moreover, we see that those at the political extremes of the spectrum remain small, e.g., from 2008 to 2020 the range was only 3–5%. One implication is that the cries of polarization are too loud. (See my recent blog post with Helmut Norpoth).6This brings me to something that keeps me up at night as a political scientist. I'm worried about the quality of the survey research that, as scholars of public opinion and voting, we routinely use. In the United States and the United Kingdom, to name two leading democratic examples, the vote intention polls pre-election have too often been grossly off, in terms of correctly identifying the winner. With respect to the US case, we recently had the surprise win of Trump in 2016 and the surprise narrow win of Biden in 2020. The prediction errors have been large and are driven by the widespread poor quality of the polls.7 The core problem rests with the increasing departure from the scientific standards of probability sampling laid down by Leslie Kish.8 In a few words, pollsters seldom sample randomly from a population list (or its equivalent), making their task one of educated guess work.MS & CT:Let's turn away from the United States for a moment. Your book Economics and Elections: The Major Western Democracies (1988) is the foundation for comparative research on voting behavior and elections. Since then, scholars have considered how political institutions, economic contexts, and social conditions impact the magnitude of the economic vote. In democratic societies, does the economy always matter for elections? How might scholars improve our comparative analysis of elections and voting?MLB:The economy is like the weather; it's always there. In democracies, the economy matters for elections.9 Of course, because the "law" of economic voting is probabilistic, its estimated economic voting coefficient may carry a somewhat different value across contests. However, the underlying process endures, e.g., the White House gains votes in the face of boom, loses votes in the face of bust. The fundamental stability of the economic vote remains a hypothesis that forever faces challenges, on the reasonable assumption that, under certain conditions, it can change significantly. With co-authors, I've looked at several of these challenges, which mostly involve specification of interaction effects. For one, we examined, comparatively, whether electoral rules, by blurring clarity of responsibility, altered the economic voting coefficient; to our surprise, it didn't.10 We also examined the notion that, because of declining party identification, the economic voting coefficient has changed; again, it didn't.11 In contrast, we did find that, contrary to conventional wisdom, the retrospective economic voter can have a long, rather than a short, time horizon, with voter evaluations "abiding."12 These "stability" challenges are worth pursuing, in the name of better theory. However, they can be hard to prove. As Blalock observed fifty years ago, at the empirical level, the linear, additive model generally serves as well as any.MS & CT:Increasing globalization reduces government control over their national economy. Do you think voters recognize this? Or will they continue to hold their national leaders responsible?MLB:Conventional wisdom suggests that globalization, by reducing government control over the economy, reduces the valence of the economic vote. This argument bases itself on the clarity of responsibility notion, which holds that unless voters see government as economically responsible they won't punish it at the ballot box. However, recent work on benchmarking, including that by Brandon Park,13 suggests that globalization has allowed voters to receive information about their "benchmark" competitors, e.g., the Poles can now easily read about how the Czechs are doing and so make a judgement about their own government's relative performance. Such findings are suggestive of how dynamic research in economics and elections continues to be.MS & CT:How has the rise in right-wing populism changed European elections and voters? How would you assess the health of democracy in Europe?MLB:About populism, there are two kinds—right-wing and left-wing. Too often, left-wing populists, a very progressive force in my view, are lumped together with right-wing populists. An ongoing concern in Europe, for some, is the growth the bureaucracy, especially the supra-national bureaucracy of the European Union. This is particularly true as the EU, the collective government apparatus informally called "Europe," intervenes more and more in domestic policy decisions, large and small, e.g., from monetary policy to how raspberry jam can be made. This type of intervention in the economy, such as budget limits and regulations, takes a form few Americans would be comfortable with. This "Europe" pressure on democracy has been much investigated by continental scholars, such as Marina Costa Lobo and the MAPLE project. Once, when Paul Krugman, Nobel Laureate, was lecturing in Spain, someone asked him what the Spanish government could do about their high level of unemployment. Krugman, a devout Keynesian, said "nothing," it's all controlled in Brussels. A political scientist might suppose, then, that democratic dissatisfaction is on the rise in Europe, out of a lost sense of participation and control. However, work I've coauthored suggests that the average European is as satisfied with the functioning of democracy in their country now, as they were ten or twenty years ago.14 In other words, no downward trend. That is surprising to me. However, it again indicates the value of comparative quantitative political science research and how it can speak authoritatively to important public policy issues.Consider the case of Denmark, in some ways a beacon of democracy for Western Europe, not to say the rest of the advanced democracies in the world.15 In what ways does democratic performance shine in that country? Denmark has managed to maintain a clear transmission of the political will of the people, as embodied in the decisions of its elected elites, in the face of tough issues such as immigration, economic growth, and climate change. This has not always been so in other Western European democracies. Take the example of France, where the political elites have tended to favor the European Union, even when important sectors of the public have hesitated to embrace it.16MS & CT:You are one of the founders and leading lights of election forecasting. What has surprised you about forecasting in political science? Why do you think it is important that political scientists make election forecasts?MLB:When I began submitting election forecasting papers in the early 1980s, scholarly journals did not take the enterprise seriously (including one editor simply returning the submission). That world no longer exists. Election forecasting has taken its place as respectable science within the discipline, becoming a growth industry. This success has had a downside, in that certain commentators, not trained in the ways of social science, have jumped on the forecasting bandwagon. title: Smith and Smitherson’s Theatre of the Absurd
abstract: Cyclic dialogue, power struggles, and comedy are all elements routinely found in absurdist theater. However, these devices may further subvert expectation and occur in surprising ways in other media, including video games. One recent, notable instance of this is 2018’s “nightmare adventure comedy” Smith and Smitherson’s Accounting+ (accountingpl.us), in which numbers are not crunched, spreadsheets are nonexistent, and hardly anything—especially regarding finances—is ever reconciled. Although the main character begins in an office, the game journeys through dreamlike settings and implicates the player in performing suggestive melodies on a sentient, conjoined xylophone of bones and summoning Satan, among other acts.Using the paradigm established by Martin Esslin in his landmark text The Theatre of the Absurd (2004), I argue that the single-player virtual reality (VR) game Accounting+ can be categorized as theatre of the absurd not only through its characters, dialogue, and story but via the medium of VR—a term rooted in the theatre and coined by drama theorist Antonin Artaud—and that VR complements (and complicates) the game’s absurdist elements by directly involving the player/actor/spectator in its actions and narrative. Through this framing of Accounting+ (A+) as theatre of the absurd (ToA) pushed to the edge of absurdity by way of VR, the limits of Esslin’s definition will be stretched in order to expand audiences’ and gamers’ understanding of the relationship of theatre and VR gaming in hopes that boundaries between entertainment, art, and play can continue to be reconsidered.For many, “virtual reality” or “VR” conjures imagery of the latest in videogame technology. Someone is wearing a headset with a sleep mask–like screen over their eyes, holding glowing wands or controllers as they punch into the air and attack enemies unseen but in-screen (or enemies that are visible if the in-screen action is being cast to a computer monitor or television for others in the room to watch). In relation to computer experiences or gaming, VR is “a hybrid performance in which human users perform ‘real interactions’ within continuous ‘real time’ and ‘real space’ (3-D) computer environments” (McKenzie 1994, 85). VR is played from a first-person perspective, so as a player nods their head up and down in real life, they simultaneously nod their character’s head up and down in VR, and what they look at in the VR world follows suit. Whereas “flat” games—think most console, computer, and phone games (but not something like Pokémon GO [an augmented reality game])—are played with more separation between the player, screen, and controls and may be played in a third-person perspective, VR games readily insert a player “into the game space as a valid and verisimilar agent of the game space” (Taylor 2003, 6). They drop the player inside the game world and into the heart of the action.The term “virtual reality” is not exclusive to computer science or video games. In fact, its beginning is directly related to theatre criticism. In The Theater and Its Double, Antonin Artaud pens what is widely recognized as its first known usage: This perpetual allusion to the materials and the principle of the theater found in almost all alchemical books should be understood as the expression of an identity (of which alchemists are extremely aware) existing between the world in which the characters, objects, images, and in a general way all that constitutes the virtual reality of the theater develops, and the purely fictitious and illusory world in which the symbols of alchemy are involved. (Artaud and Richards 1958, 49) Here, virtual reality is not intended to allude to any simulated computer realities but to the simulated reality of the theatre. In the context of each play, this virtual reality is constituted by way of plot, dialogue, mise-en-scène, and other devices. Although a virtual reality can be created onstage, making it part of, next to, and/or housed within our physical reality, the lines of physical reality are blurred and crossed by the virtual, which is a world apart operating on its own terms.In “Ludic Identities and the Magic Circle,” Gordon Calleja interrogates Johan Huizinga’s similar notion of the “magic circle,” which asserts that “the act of game playing requires the crossing of the boundary that marks the game from the ordinary world” (2015, 211). This boundary, known as the “magic circle,” separates the game world from quotidian life and distinguishes game rules, norms, and possibilities from those of day-to-day existence. The magic circle is a partner concept to virtual reality, and it comes as no surprise that even the language Artaud uses to describe virtual reality borrows from that of the alchemical or magical. Arguably, though virtual reality can be distinguished from other parts of the ordinary world, that does not necessarily mean the edges of its magic circle are impermeable via immersion and performance, as evidenced in VR gaming.A main component to virtual reality is its ability to encapsulate a user in an experience so they feel as if they are one with the VR world, and this is more quickly accomplished in VR gaming due to its nature of fostering immersion and associated experiential aspects. One key factor of immersion deals less with the “illusion” of a virtual world and more with “indicat[ing] a specific kind of spatial relationship between a body and an environment,” melding the qualities of relative scale—an “environment must be construed as larger than the object it is to encompass”—and proximity—“there must be contact, or the prospect of contact, between a body and its environment”—to forge a multidimensional relationship between the two that results in immersion (Rogers 2019, 139). This factor speaks to the understood size and physicality of a VR environment. If a player, who is situated in physical reality, wearing a VR headset with two small screens in front of their eyes, feels as though that VR world is much bigger than the size of their own body and real-life room; like they are standing, floating, or flying within that world; and as if they can reach out to touch pieces of the environment, then the physical/spatial requirement of VR immersion has been achieved.As for the “illusion” of a virtual realm, in “Immersion vs. Interactivity: Virtual Reality and Literary Theory,” Marie-Laure Ryan investigates immersion and its related concepts as they apply to gaming, outlining how these principles work together to create virtual realities. Interactivity is the first building block and relates to the power of a player to modify their virtual environment—“the virtual world must respond to the user’s actions” (Ryan 1999, 121). According to Ryan, “Meaningful interactivity requires a compromise between range and mapping and between discovery and predictability,” and a virtual reality of a well-designed game is essentially antithetical to our everyday, chaotic realism (124). Although the actions a player can take may be varied and complex, there are not infinite types of interactions, and the possible in-game interactions tend toward those that shepherd a player to the creator’s or designer’s goal. Interactivity, when implemented well and combined with other factors, can lead to immersion—a sense of being present in and part of the magic circle—but immersion would not be possible without some level of interactivity. Part of what contributes to a strong sense of immersion is that a player must be able to traverse their virtual reality, to move around in it, to affect change and be affected by changes.Similarly, the parallel concepts of performance and transportation involve players participating in gameplay with the commitment of actors on a stage—creating and becoming part of a performance—which leads them to move away from the surroundings of their physical reality and lose themselves in the unfolding events—a sensation called transportation (Ryan 1999, 116). When a player is both immersed in or transported to a virtual reality and actively engaging with it—actively interacting and performing with the environment, characters, objects—then a feeling of telepresence is fostered. Telepresence is akin to being in the center of the magic circle, so to speak. Ryan describes it as feeling present in a mediated environment rather than the “everyday” physical reality (111). The virtual reality becomes one’s present reality and is (very nearly) separated from “the real world.” Like interactivity leading to immersion or performance leading to transportation and telepresence, in “Experience, 60 Frames Per Second,” Chris Alton posits that engagement with the VR environment leads to embodiment (2017, 223). Virtual embodiment is defined as an “in-the-moment, sense experience tying body and mind together,” and it “entails the bodily reactions and sensations which come from this digital immersion” (215). In immersive VR gaming, body and mind react to a player’s virtual reality as if it were the “base” reality outside of the headset and VR realm. It is this reality-blurring suspension of disbelief, which will further be referred to as “immersion” more comprehensively, that helps tie a VR game like Accounting+ to theory of performance and theatre of the absurd.At this point, linguistic parallels between videogaming and the theatre may have already come to mind. A synonym for an actor is a “player,” recalling the notion of the human “player(s)” of a video game who act upon and within game environments. Characters inhabit theatre just as in video games, some of which are background actors of a play or nonplayable characters (NPCs) in the background of a game who cannot be interacted with at all (as opposed to minor characters or NPCs with whom the player can interact). The list could—and does—go on, but these parallels exist because theatre and games are both performance activities, and by using performance frameworks VR gaming can be further situated as an immersive activity that takes place within a (malleable) magic circle.In “Play’s the Thing: A Framework to Study Videogames as Performance,” Clara Fernández-Vara outlines the basic qualities of performance and how they apply not only to theatre, but also to gaming. Performance, whether in relationship to theatre or VR gaming, can be understood “as a process of making meaning on the part of the originators of the activity and their audience” (Fernández-Vara 2009, 1). Theatre actors are performers, sure, but videogame players are performers as well, serving as co-creative participants or “originators of activity” by physically and/or vocally interacting with input devices to create action on screen and in the virtual environment. By way of game creators and programmers, NPCs performing actions—even though scripted and coded into the game—can contribute to the performance process. “The human performance becomes immersed within or surrounded by the computer performance” (McKenzie 1994, 86) as NPCs’ actions, interactions, and reactions aid in the player’s understanding and meaning making.Audience is an essential part of this definition of performance, too, as the action and the meaning of the In video games, in of the The player parallels both the of the theatre play, and of the of The player is an because is also an but is also the of the performance, is the one who sense of the and The of the game and specific are also part of the experience of the player as of own (Fernández-Vara 2009, The is their own and actions and the environment as it also other NPCs in the of games or those within of the and human can two on the the player, a of an or from the world via can be immersed in in ways both (as in the of theatre or and being in a away from the this in and the of by that through the work it requires of may be a that is able to the to a virtual the activity of game playing into characters who exist in the virtual of video games, theatre and the activity in to a performance into characters who exist in the of the a play to some that they are a play, just as a player would be that there is a level of separation between themselves and a VR realm. title: Dialogues: anthropology and literature
abstract: The relationship between anthropology and literature has attracted renewed theoretical energy in recent years (Brandel 2020; Debaene 2014; Fassin 2014; Reed 2018; Wulff 2016), developing and deepening connections with, for example, anthropological theories of art (Reed 2011), religion (Furani 2012), subjectivity (Olszewska 2015), and ethics (Bush 2017), as well as with allied fields and traditions, including postcolonial theory (Sadana 2012), Bourdieuan sociology (Dalsgård 2021), media theory (Rosen 2022), and ordinary language philosophy (Brandel 2023). Among the most fruitful trends in current research has been a revitalized emphasis on the possibilities for collaboration between writers and anthropologists, which has generated critical debate on the ethical and political limits of conventional methodologies (Schielke & Shehata 2021). The following set of conversations reflect and refract these trends in different ways, while proposing further openings for future work, particularly around questions of translation, creativity, care, and particularity. Each of these dialogues took place between anthropologists and writers with long-standing relationships, as members of collaborative research teams, co-authors, companions, mentors, and fieldwork interlocutors. Their differences in form reflect their range of commitments and approaches to the study of creative language practices. title: “They Have Received Many Wounds”: Applying a Trauma-Informed Lens to The Book of Mormon
abstract: The field of biblical studies has made significant inroads in understanding scripture through a trauma hermeneutic in recent years, with efficacious results.2 Biblical interpreters using the lens of trauma have drawn on the fields of psychology, sociology, comparative literature, and refugee studies to understand scriptural text in new ways. A trauma hermeneutic (or trauma-informed lens or reading) not only recognizes the ways in which the experience of trauma immediately affects individuals but also how trauma ripples through generations and communities and how the text may reflect the effects of unprocessed trauma and play a role in healing from traumatic events. Rather than a single method of interpretation, the field of biblical trauma studies has created a “frame of reference” that draws on many different trauma theories and is intended to be coupled with other diverse forms of biblical criticism.3 It is “a fluid orientation, or sensitivity in reading with different possible emphases.”4 Yet this “heuristic framework”5 has been severely underutilized in readings of the Book of Mormon, a scriptural text that contains an abundance of stories of traumatic events. Two important exceptions to this are in the work of Deidre Green and Kylie Nielson Turley, both of whom have brilliantly used a trauma-informed hermeneutic to yield fascinating insights into the characters of Jacob and Alma.6 This article will explain what trauma is and how to be trauma informed, describe a few examples from the Book of Mormon in which a sensitivity to trauma could reveal greater insights from the text, and argue for the importance of using a trauma hermeneutic. We conclude with an application of a trauma hermeneutic in religious settings and an argument for the importance of being aware of how scriptural trauma may interact with the potential trauma of readers.The word “trauma” has become a modern buzzword, often applied to contexts or situations without a clear understanding of the term. Literally “wound” in Greek, trauma can be physical, such as the physical trauma to our organs resulting from a bullet wound, or psychological, such as the mental and emotional trauma we carry with us after an upsetting or violent event. Trauma “results from an event, series of events, or set of circumstances that is experienced by an individual as physically or emotionally harmful or threatening and that has lasting adverse effects on the individual's functioning and physical, social, emotional, or spiritual well-being.”7 Psychological trauma, the focus of this article, can be understood by examining (1) the event, (2) how it is experienced, and (3) its effects.8Trauma can occur on a macro or micro scale. Macrotraumatic events (also called communal trauma) simultaneously impact a large group or a society, introducing long-term consequences with which members of the group must grapple with for many years. These include natural disasters, wars, mass shootings, pandemics, and other violent or destructive events with the power to upend many lives. They can also include institutional action or inaction, such as a church or university covering up abuse or failing to protect marginalized individuals.9 Though the situations at the heart of such institutional trauma may directly impact only a small number of individuals (e.g., those abused by persons in power), the implications of an institution protecting abusers or failing to act when its members were harmed can trigger ripples of distress, harm, and distrust across the institution, leading to a macrotraumatic event. Microtraumatic events hold the same power to upend lives and destroy mental health as the macro events, though these typically impact a smaller number of people at once. Micro traumas can include familial events such as abuse, death, or divorce; experiences of or exposures to community violence such as assault, exploitation, or bullying; or any other interpersonal or individual event that causes injury, shame, or other physical or psychological harm for those involved.10Trauma can also be passed intergenerationally in various pathways, including biochemically, culturally, and narratively. Biochemically, trauma can be inherited via epigenetic effects wherein markers at the chromosomal level are passed across the generations. Culturally, it may be taught via parenting practices or familial expectations. These pathways may be closely intertwined. title: Proportion, Perspective, and Number in The Parlement of the Thre Ages
abstract: However the problem is defined, the critics agree. The knitting together of conventional elements in the Middle English Parlement of the Thre Ages lacks unity, or a proper sense of proportion, or stylistic consistency. Its poet's awkward manner of combining sections is always called its most confusing and least successful aspect, even while readers generally agree that the alliterative poem possesses many charming bits as it works its way toward a message of life's pleasures inevitably ending in death. In themselves, the poem's dream-vision structure and plot are simple and uncomplicated. Parlement opens with a hunt in the month of May. A solitary narrator stalks a magnificent stag, royal in bearing; kills it with a well-aimed arrow; and then formally brittles the creature in the aristocratic manner also detailed in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (providing a valuable analogue to the greater poem). After hiding his conquest, the narrator feels the sun's direct warmth, falls asleep, and envisions in his “saule” (l. 103) the numerically aged Three Ages in personified form: Youthe, 30; Medill Elde, 60; Elde, 100.1 Youthe, a splendid Pride of Life figure, exudes a perpetual springtime of vigor, accoutered with fashionable clothes, beautiful things, love, romance, and carefree leisure. Autumnal Medill Elde, a sterner, more avaricious figure, frets over keeping what he has gained in life—property, lands, livestock, profits. They engage in debate, with Youthe speaking more, celebrating falconry in a beautiful passage, and “winning” simply by being so glowingly attractive in his moment of life.Then Elde, a decrepit figure, halts the squabble of Youthe and Medill Elde by launching into a historical discourse on the Nine Worthies: the pagans Hector, Alexander, and Caesar; the Jews Joshua, David, and Judas Maccabeus; and the Christians Arthur, Godfrey of Bouillon, and Charlemagne. Here is where most modern readers feel Parlement's disunity begin to set in, because the first two Ages now withdraw, never to speak again, and Elde talks on and on, not merely recounting his uneven tales of the Worthies, but also adding more rosters of model humans: the freshly invented Four Wisemen (Aristotle, Virgil, Solomon, Merlin) and Sixteen Lovers. Elde starts and ends his long speech by naming a fourth personification, Death, who hovers marginally behind a figurative door: “Dethe dynges one my dore” (l. 654; also l. 292). When Elde finally falls silent, the blast of a horn startles the narrator awake; whether it sounds in the dream or in the waking world is ambiguous. The narrator hastens out of the forest and back to town, now in a prayerful mood and aware of life's vanity and brevity. His adventure began just before dawn and now the sun has set.2 The action of hunt and sleep occupies a day under the sun—a figurative lifespan as implied by Elde's sign-off, “haues gude daye” (l. 653), and the narrator's closing prayer, “dere Drightyne this daye dele vs of thi blysse” (l. 664).Parlement sports conventions that were richly enjoyed by late medieval aristocratic audiences: a springtime setting, a hunt, an expert carving of the game, a dream with personifications, an allegorical dispute, the Nine Worthies.3 Despite these contemporary crowd-pleasers, Parlement has not garnered the ongoing scrutiny or steady cycles of fresh critical response that would mark it as a great Middle English poem by modern standards. In this, it differs markedly from comparable works in its unrhymed alliterative meter, poems such as Gawain, Piers Plowman, Morte Arthure, Saint Erkenwald, and Wynnere and Wastoure. Parlement's history of criticism has always proceeded slowly, with little appearing after its first edition in 1915 by Sir Israel Gollancz, and the pace picking up only gradually after M. Y. Offord's 1959 EETS edition.4 Its critical heyday began around 1966, peaked in the 1970s and 80s, but after 1989 has slowed to a mere dribble.5 In 1930, well before Offord's edition, the first substantial assessment of Parlement appeared (notably) in the pages of this journal. title: Soslowsky Sentiments: H. R. Lissner Medal Presentation
abstract: This article generally reproduces the presentation given by the author at the 2018 World Congress of Biomechanics in Dublin, Ireland in recognition of his receipt of the H.R. Lissner Medal from the American Society of Mechanical Engineers. This paper discusses my family, followed by my undergraduate and graduate experiences at Columbia University. It then reviews some activities during my first faculty position at the University of Michigan and then continues on with my experiences over the past 20+ years at the University of Pennsylvania. I review the programmatic approaches I have taken that have resulted in a publication history in different, but related areas, as well as future plans. I describe the graduate students, other trainees, staff, and environment that have made my efforts so enjoyable and gratifying. I then note some of the additional leadership positions I have had the good fortune to experience along the way thus far. I conclude by speaking briefly about my close partners and mentors, as well as some key takeaways from my experience.I am truly humbled and honored to receive this award. I begin by acknowledging and recognizing the amazing history of H. R. Lissner Medal recipients starting in 1977 and going through the present (Table 1). This list represents a literal “who's who” in the field of biomechanics and to think my name will join that list feels a bit strange. I would like to call special attention to three of the previous recipients because they each played a central role in my professional development and I will discuss them in this paper: first, Richard Skalak (1985) for whom I worked as an undergraduate student; second, Van Mow (1987) my Ph.D. thesis advisor; and third, Steve Goldstein (2005) who hired me for my first tenure track faculty position.I want to start by acknowledging my family. My parents Phyllis and Martin shown here at their wedding in 1959 (Fig. 1) have been amazing pillars of strength, love, and support for me in everything that I have tried to do from my earliest memories. My parents and my sister Sandy formed a very loving and nurturing household (Fig. 2). I am truly lucky to have grown up with this amazing family.My undergraduate experience was at Columbia University in New York and I had the great fortune to meet Professor Richard Skalak at the beginning of my sophomore year in 1983. Professor Skalak was the James Kip Finch Professor and Director of the Bioengineering Institute at Columbia (this was long before there was a Department of Biomedical Engineering). He hired me then as his first work-study student and I began working in his office for a part-time job (I worked in the main university library as a freshman). My experience with Professor Skalak was my greatest opportunity and fortune. When people ask me how and why I am in the field, my answer is simple. For many, the answer is multifactorial. It was a personal injury that got me interested, coupled with a work experience, coupled with a class exercise, coupled with something else. For me…, it was Richard Skalak (period). Early on in my time with him, he and Professor Shu Chien were editors for the Handbook of Bioengineering to be published by McGraw-Hill. This book was to have over 40 chapters written by the greats of the field in bioengineering. In fact, many of the authors were, or went on to be, Lissner Medal honorees. This job required me to read each chapter's draft and proofread for consistency or clarity. Then, I was to contact each of these authors with questions related to their figures, layout, or other matters. In summary, they actually PAID ME to learn about the field and be introduced to the greats of the field. This opportunity was nothing short of amazing!We worked on this project with Professor Shu Chien whom we met many times up at Columbia's Medical School and who was a great partner for this book. I was really honored that they put this acknowledgment to me in the Handbook of Bioengineering Preface “We also acknowledge with thanks, the very competent and thorough assistance of Louis Soslowsky in proofreading and coordinating manuscripts at Columbia University. His help has facilitated the progress of this project greatly.” They also wrote a small note inside on the cover of the version of the book that I have in my office today: “With many thanks and best regards” and “With appreciation and best wishes” and this was very meaningful to me as a simple undergraduate student, coming from such luminaries in the field (Fig. 3).As I continued on my undergraduate years working for Professor Skalak, I was fortunate to be able to move “out of the office” and into a research project. I published my first full-length paper titled “Theory of filtration of mixed blood suspensions.” Professor Skalak was the first author, Professor Chien was the last author, and I was the second author. This paper presented a theory for flow of suspensions of blood cells and demonstrated that small concentrations of stiff cells dominated the response. Although I enjoyed this work quite a bit and it allowed me to experience the excitement of publishing as an undergraduate, I was not as interested in blood flow for my Ph.D. thesis. At that time, Professor Skalak introduced me to Professor Van C. Mow who had just been recruited to Columbia from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in 1986. This is a photo from Dr. Skalak's 70th birthday symposium in San Diego and an opportunity for me to be with them both together (Fig. 4).My graduate school years were amazing and the environment that Dr. Mow created for all of us was something we did not truly appreciate or recognize at the time, but it was surely nothing short of brilliance. Shown here is a photo of the lab personnel in approximately 1988 (Fig. 5). The papers that I published during my Ph.D. thesis were mostly related to joint mechanics, some stereophotogrammetry with Gerard Ateshian quantifying the shape of the shoulder surfaces as well as joint contact patterns at both the glenohumeral joint and the subacromial space, as well as measuring the mechanical properties of the inferior glenohumeral ligament. This last paper is still my most highly cited today. We had the great fortune to be well integrated with orthopedic surgeon colleagues Evan Flatow, Roger Pollock, and Lou Bigliani. Those years were truly formative for me and these are people that I still speak with today from literally more than 30 years. The group of graduate students we had was truly unbelievable as well, and again, I wish we would have realized at the time how amazing this group was: Farshid Guilak, Kerry Athanasiou, Lori Setton, Gerard Ateshian, Weiyong Gu, Wenbo Zhu, and others. We were very close friends at the time in graduate school and we realized we had something special but not to the extent we realize now.After my graduate school years in 1991, I was recruited to the University of Michigan by Professor Steve Goldstein. Steve contacted me before I was really beginning to think about faculty jobs and offered me the opportunity to come out and visit. I have to confess that I only went to visit for what I called “interview practice” as I had never lived west of New Jersey to that time and I was not sure that I ever would. Steve Goldstein was very sincere, and I was impressed by the environment he had created and the opportunity that the University would likely afford me. I did accept the faculty position at that time as I was so impressed by the people and the environment (probably the only thing that really matters when looking for a first faculty job). Interestingly, I accepted the position with a start-up package of a handshake from Steve. He explained that he would be supportive of me and would do everything he could to help me be successful. I could have the existing lab staff assist me as I needed and use the equipment that was already in place. There were no dollar amounts and no written multiyear commitment. It was a good firm handshake and a gentlemen's understanding. I trusted Steve, and although I would take that job again in a heartbeat, I would not recommend anyone today to take a job on a handshake; rather, spend time thinking about what you will need, consult peers and mentors, and for certain, get everything in writing. At Michigan, I was introduced to three orthopedic surgeons that I worked closely with, all of whom I still speak with today: Ralph Blasier, Jim Carpenter, and Jed Kuhn. During that time, we embarked on a series of studies in shoulder joint mechanics that represented more than 40 full length papers over the years. These studies included defining changes in ligament properties with rotator cuff tears to finding those factors that stabilized the shoulder joint in different directions, as well as measuring strain fields in the glenohumeral capsule under different loading conditions. Another series of papers that I began at that time were elucidating structure-function relationships in tendon and I published over 50 papers in this space over the years. I should mention that many of these paper topics overlap, with some of the structure-function relationship papers, for example, related to the shoulder. We began classic structure-function studies in a controlled tendon fascicle model, considering the role of glycosaminoglycans and their chain lengths in structure-function. We developed and used an optical strain system building on the previous systems popularized by Dr. Savio Woo for our field. At this time, I began the use of transgenic mouse models, starting with the Mov13 mouse and moving on to the decorin knockout mouse and then several others. I believe that these might have been the earliest use of a transgenic or knockout model in the tendon field. We then began studies in the rat rotator cuff and published more than 100 papers to date using the rat rotator cuff models. We submitted our first Orthopaedic Research Society abstract on the rat rotator cuff model in 1993 (25 years ago!), presented it at the annual meeting in 1994, and published our first full-length paper with this model in 1996.
